[ANSWER]: Fairness in machine learning has been conceptualized along two complementary dimensions.  Individual fairness emphasizes that similar individuals should receive similar outcomes, often operationalized through similarity metrics defined over feature spaces.  Group fairness, by contrast, requires statistical parity or equality of treatment across predefined demographic groups, typically expressed as constraints on aggregate quantities such as mean predictions or error rates.  Early formulations of these notions laid the groundwork for a broad literature that explores trade‑offs between them and investigates how each can be quantified and enforced.

A large body of work focuses on modifying the data before model training (pre‑processing).  Techniques in this category aim to transform the input distribution so that protected attributes become statistically independent of the features or labels, thereby reducing the potential for biased predictions.  Representative approaches include re‑weighting schemes, latent representation learning, and generative models that produce debiased synthetic data.  These methods are motivated by the desire to eliminate bias at its source, but they often require access to the entire dataset and may alter information that is predictive for the downstream task.

Another prominent line of research modifies model outputs after training (post‑processing).  Post‑processing methods keep the original classifier fixed and adjust its predictions to satisfy fairness constraints, for example by thresholding scores differently across groups or by applying calibrated probability shifts.  Such techniques are attractive because they can be applied to any pretrained model without retraining, yet they may sacrifice predictive performance and can be limited in the types of fairness constraints they can accommodate.

In‑processing approaches intervene directly during model training, incorporating fairness considerations into the learning objective or the optimization procedure.  Early in‑processing methods introduced regularizers or constraints based on statistical parity, equalized odds, or disparate impact, and they often employ convex surrogates to enable tractable optimization.  Some strategies explicitly project an unfair model onto a feasible set defined by fairness constraints, using divergences such as the Kullback‑Leibler (KL) divergence to measure the distance between the original and projected models.  These projection‑based methods provide a principled way to balance accuracy and fairness but can be computationally demanding when the constraint set is complex.

Optimal transport (OT) has emerged as a powerful tool for measuring discrepancies between probability distributions, and several recent works have applied OT concepts to fairness.  A common theme in this literature is the use of Wasserstein barycenters to construct a “fair” distribution that is equidistant from the empirical distributions of each demographic group.  Barycenter‑based techniques have been employed for preprocessing (to align group distributions), for classification (to adjust decision boundaries), and for regression (to modify predicted values).  While intuitive for a small number of groups, these methods rely on explicit equality constraints across groups, limiting their flexibility when handling multiple or continuous sensitive attributes and imposing the requirement that the transport cost be a true metric.

A related strand of research investigates direct OT projections onto fairness‑constrained sets without resorting to barycenters.  One notable approach computes an unregularized OT projection of a classifier’s score function onto the set of functions that satisfy prescribed group fairness constraints, using the resulting transport cost as a diagnostic of unfairness.  This line of work demonstrates the feasibility of measuring unfairness via OT but does not provide an efficient, differentiable regularizer that can be integrated into standard training pipelines.

In contrast, the present contribution introduces a novel optimal‑transport‑based fairness regularizer that quantifies the minimal transport cost required to transform a probabilistic classifier into any function satisfying a broad class of linear fairness constraints.  By incorporating entropic regularization, the method yields a differentiable surrogate that can be added to arbitrary loss functions, enabling end‑to‑end training of fair models.  The formulation accommodates multiple sensitive attributes—both categorical and continuous—and supports complex linear constraints beyond simple parity or equalized odds.  An efficient algorithmic scheme is derived to compute the regularized transport cost, and empirical evaluations demonstrate that the approach achieves a superior trade‑off between predictive performance and group fairness compared with existing pre‑, post‑, and in‑processing techniques, as well as with prior OT‑based methods.

[ANSWER]: Analyzing the expressive power of coupling‑based normalizing flows has attracted considerable attention. Early universality results established that any coupling flow capable of approximating an arbitrary invertible map can represent any target density weakly [1]. This line of work was later extended to specific architectures such as affine couplings [2, 3, 4], Flow++ [5], neural autoregressive flows [6] and SOS‑polynomial flows [7]. While these studies demonstrate weak or Wasserstein convergence, they rely on increasingly ill‑conditioned transformations—functions become highly discontinuous as the approximation error shrinks—whereas empirical practice shows that learned couplings remain smooth. Moreover, the convergence criteria used (weak convergence or Wasserstein distance) do not guarantee reduction of the maximum‑likelihood loss that practitioners actually optimize. An arbitrarily small distance in those metrics can still correspond to an infinite Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. In contrast, the present work directly tackles the KL divergence: we decompose the loss into a non‑Gaussianity term and a non‑Standardness term, and we prove quantitative convergence of the latter. This yields the first linear‑rate bound on KL‑based convergence for generic coupling‑based flows, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical guarantees and the loss employed in practice.

Subsequent investigations have examined conditions under which well‑conditioned couplings suffice. For instance, it was shown that well‑conditioned affine couplings can approximate log‑concave padded distributions, albeit again measured in Wasserstein distance [9]. Lipschitz‑constrained flows were found to be unable to capture arbitrary tail behavior, a limitation that can be mitigated by modifying the latent prior [10]. Although SOS‑polynomial flows achieve total‑variation convergence [11] and zero‑padded affine couplings converge weakly [12], none of these results address KL convergence. By focusing on the KL divergence, our analysis complements these findings and clarifies that well‑conditioned couplings can already guarantee meaningful progress on the maximum‑likelihood objective without resorting to pathological conditioning.

A particularly relevant line of work demonstrated that a stack of 48 linear affine coupling blocks can represent any invertible linear map [8], which in turn implies that any Gaussian can be transformed into a standard normal. Building on this observation, we reinterpret the result in terms of the KL loss decomposition introduced above. Our theory shows that the “non‑Standardness” component of the KL divergence contracts at a linear rate with depth, implying that far fewer layers than the 48‑block construction are needed to achieve a comparable KL reduction for typical flow architectures. This positions our contribution as a refinement of existing linear‑algebraic universality statements, providing practical depth estimates that align with the loss actually minimized during training.

While these approaches have demonstrated improvements in sentence ordering [4], emotion recognition [5], story generation [6, 7] and dialogue generation [8], they operate on knowledge that is largely detached from the surrounding discourse. In contrast, our contribution is a dialogue‑centric dataset that supplies fine‑grained, utterance‑level commonsense inferences grounded explicitly in conversational context, thereby addressing the mismatch between context‑free knowledge and discourse‑level reasoning.

ConceptNet captures generic relational facts between entities but ignores the linguistic and situational context in which those entities appear. Consequently, models that rely solely on ConceptNet often miss the nuanced cues required for reasoning across multiple turns of a dialogue. By curating CICERO, we provide a resource where each inference is tied to the specific conversational history that gave rise to it, enabling models to learn context‑sensitive commonsense reasoning that goes beyond the entity‑level associations of ConceptNet.

COMET [10] extends the utility of CSKBs by learning to generate commonsense triples for a given sentence, yet its training data are derived from the same static knowledge bases and therefore lack the richness of real conversational exchanges. Our approach circumvents this limitation by directly annotating dyadic dialogues with five distinct inference types (cause, subsequent event, prerequisite, motivation, and emotional reaction), furnishing models with examples of how commonsense manifests in natural, multi‑turn interactions rather than in isolated sentences.

This broader coverage enables models to reason about the antecedents and affective consequences of utterances, aspects that GLUCOSE does not address.

[ANSWER]: Metric learning seeks a distance function that brings semantically similar examples together while pushing dissimilar ones apart. In deep metric learning, an explicit non‑linear mapping from raw inputs to a low‑dimensional embedding space is learned, after which Euclidean distance exhibits the desired behavior. Although unsupervised formulations exist, the majority of work follows a supervised paradigm in which positive pairs share a class label and negative pairs belong to different classes. Loss functions for deep metric learning can be categorized as pair‑based or proxy‑based. Pair‑based losses operate on direct relationships between data points and have been defined over pairs, triplets, quadruplets, or higher‑order tuples. These losses capture fine‑grained data‑to‑data relations but are sensitive to label noise and outliers, and they often contain terms that become inactive once constraints are satisfied, yielding zero gradients. Consequently, hard‑example mining strategies such as semi‑hard or distance‑weighted sampling are commonly employed to provide informative training signals. Proxy‑based losses introduce learnable class proxies in the embedding space, replacing data‑to‑data interactions with data‑to‑proxy relations. By summarizing global class structure, proxy‑based approaches reduce computational overhead, generate more consistently non‑zero gradients, and typically require less aggressive mining, leading to faster convergence.

Input mixup linearly interpolates between two or more examples in the input space to augment data. Numerous extensions exploit the structure of specific domains, particularly images, by performing non‑linear interpolations or applying mixup to transformed representations. Manifold mixup extends the idea to intermediate feature representations, sometimes coupled with decoding back to the input space. In both input‑ and feature‑level mixup, target labels are interpolated linearly, and most studies have focused on cross‑entropy loss for classification tasks. The application of mixup to pairwise loss functions, such as those used in metric learning, has received considerably less attention.

Within deep metric learning, several works have explored interpolation strategies compatible with pairwise objectives. Embedding expansion and symmetrical synthesis interpolate pairs of embeddings deterministically within the same class, making them applicable to pair‑based losses. Proxy synthesis, on the other hand, interpolates between class proxies and can be used with proxy‑based losses; however, it does not modify labels, which can lead to the inadvertent creation of false negatives when the interpolation factor approaches the extremes. In contrastive representation learning, MoCHi interpolates anchor embeddings with negative samples without altering labels and employs a threshold to mitigate false negatives. A similar thresholding concept appears in OptTransMix, which adjusts interpolation to avoid label ambiguity. The i‑mix approach interpolates anchor embeddings along with their virtual class labels in a linear fashion; it maintains a single positive per anchor while keeping all negatives clean, thereby limiting its ability to exploit interpolation for relative weighting of positives and negatives. These methods collectively illustrate a growing interest in leveraging interpolation for metric‑learning objectives, while highlighting challenges related to label handling and the balance between positive and negative contributions.

Our contribution inverts this perspective: we deliberately inject a confounder into each image so that the resulting spurious association prevents the model from learning the genuine mapping, thereby turning a traditionally negative phenomenon into a privacy‑preserving mechanism. [ANSWER]: Bootstrapping was first introduced in the reinforcement‑learning literature through temporal‑difference (TD) methods, where an agent uses its own future predictions as targets to learn value functions [1].  More recent work has adapted the same principle to self‑supervised settings, employing learned predictions as training signals without external supervision [2, 3].

In multi‑task meta‑learning, several approaches meta‑learn an initialization for stochastic gradient descent by minimizing the Euclidean distance between the adapted parameters and the task‑optimal parameters [4, 5].  This “target‑matching’’ idea has been extended to broader self‑referential meta‑learning frameworks in which the meta‑learned update rule is itself used to optimise the meta‑objective [6, 7].

Matching parameters under a Kullback‑Leibler (KL) divergence is closely related to knowledge‑distillation techniques, where a student network is trained to imitate a teacher network.  In many distillation setups the teacher is either a fixed expert or a moving aggregation of experts [8, 9, 10, 3], whereas other methods generate targets by following a prescribed update rule rather than by aggregating existing models.

Trust‑region methods introduce an explicit distance function to regularize gradient updates, thereby controlling the step size and curvature of the optimisation landscape [11, 12, 13, 14].  These techniques have been applied in both supervised and reinforcement‑learning contexts to improve stability and convergence.

Prior work such as Dwivedi et al. identified inconsistent experimental configurations that lead to unreliable comparisons, while Shchur et al. demonstrated that reusing identical train‑test splits induces overfitting and can flip method rankings. The Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) later responded by offering diverse datasets together with unified splits and metrics to improve reproducibility. Building on this line of inquiry, our study extends the scrutiny to dynamic link prediction, where the evaluation challenges are even more pronounced. By designing stricter negative‑sampling protocols, introducing a memorization‑based baseline, and releasing six new dynamic datasets, we provide a complementary suite of tools that address the specific shortcomings of current dynamic‑graph benchmarks.

Research on dynamic graphs has largely concentrated on differentiating dynamic from static link prediction (e.g., Junuthula et al.) and on leveraging auxiliary information such as friendship networks to improve future‑link forecasts. Comprehensive surveys (e.g., Haghani and Keyvanpour) have categorized dynamic link prediction into missing‑link and future‑link tasks, but they stop short of questioning the adequacy of existing evaluation pipelines. In contrast, our work adopts a different perspective: we keep the task definition unchanged but fundamentally reshape the evaluation landscape. Our two novel negative‑sampling strategies—historical and inductive—target the bias introduced by easy negatives, while EdgeBank, a simple memorization baseline, highlights how current protocols can be inadvertently over‑optimistic. Moreover, by curating datasets from politics, economics, and transportation, we broaden the domain coverage beyond the socially‑biased benchmarks that dominate prior studies.

Negative sampling has long been recognized as a critical component of graph representation learning. Early approaches for static link prediction relied on uniformly random negatives, whereas later methods introduced degree‑aware or distance‑aware schemes to generate harder examples. Empirical analyses by Kotnis and Nastase showed that training‑time negative‑sampling choices can markedly affect learned embeddings in knowledge‑graph settings. However, the impact of negative sampling during **evaluation** has received little attention. Our contribution fills this gap by systematically investigating how different test‑time negative‑sampling strategies influence reported performance. The historical and inductive samplers we propose are specifically engineered for dynamic graphs, leveraging edge‑recurrence patterns to produce challenging negatives that better discriminate among competing models. This advances the state of the art beyond existing static‑focused sampling heuristics and aligns evaluation more closely with real‑world deployment scenarios.

The rapid growth of dynamic graph representation learning has produced a rich ecosystem of temporal graph neural networks, from early surveys by Kazemi et al. and Skardinga et al. to concrete architectures such as JODIE, DyRep, TGAT, TGN, and CAWN. While these models have reported near‑perfect link‑prediction scores on popular benchmarks, such results often stem from evaluation protocols that fail to stress the models with difficult negatives or diverse graph domains. Our experiments confirm that, under the proposed harder negative‑sampling regimes and on the newly introduced multi‑domain datasets, the apparent superiority of many existing DGNNs diminishes, exposing the need for more rigorous assessment. Consequently, our work not only supplies stronger baselines and richer datasets but also redefines the evaluation standards that future dynamic‑graph research should adopt.

[ANSWER]: The problem of differentially private selection and the exponential mechanism have been investigated extensively in the literature, with numerous analyses of their theoretical properties, implementations, and applications across a wide range of domains [1–13].

A frequently used alternative to the exponential mechanism is the report‑noisy‑max technique, which perturbs each quality score with noise and returns the item with the largest noisy score. Empirical studies have shown that report‑noisy‑max can be competitive with the exponential mechanism, but the two methods do not dominate each other in a Pareto sense: report‑noisy‑max performs better on certain score vectors, while the exponential mechanism is superior on others. Several additional mechanisms have been proposed for private selection that exploit specific assumptions or special cases, offering improved utility under those conditions [2,5–9].

To address settings where quality scores have heterogeneous sensitivity, a generalization of the exponential mechanism was introduced in [10]. This approach constructs a modified quality function that balances the raw score against its sensitivity and then applies the exponential mechanism to the transformed function, thereby preserving differential privacy while adapting to varying sensitivities. Separate work [11] refined the privacy analysis of multiple sequential executions of the exponential mechanism, showing that leveraging the range of the score function rather than its sensitivity can tighten composition bounds. These refinements are orthogonal to the core selection mechanism and can be incorporated into alternative designs.

When the quality functions themselves are differentially private mechanisms, a distinct selection problem arises. Study [12] presented a mechanism that operates on such private candidates, removing the need for bounded‑sensitivity assumptions on the scores. This formulation is particularly relevant for applications like hyper‑parameter optimization, where the scores are derived from private learning procedures.

The optimality of the exponential mechanism has also been examined. In [3] the authors formulated linear‑programming characterizations of mechanisms that are optimal on average, focusing on graph‑structured input–output universes where each node corresponds to a database. They proved that any optimal mechanism must satisfy privacy constraints with equality on adjacent nodes and that the exponential mechanism attains optimality up to a constant factor of two in this setting.

Beyond private selection, a line of research has derived optimal mechanisms for other privacy‑constrained tasks by carefully analyzing the underlying constraints. Results include optimal constructions for predicate‑counting queries [15], mechanisms that achieve information‑theoretic limits under differential privacy [16], and generic approaches for low‑sensitivity functions [17].

Building on this body of work, we introduce the permute‑and‑flip mechanism as a drop‑in replacement for the exponential mechanism in the private selection problem. The new mechanism retains the simplicity, linear‑time runtime, and ease of implementation of the exponential mechanism while guaranteeing that its expected utility is never lower and can be up to twice as high. By explicitly respecting the privacy constraints, the permute‑and‑flip mechanism is Pareto optimal among selection mechanisms and, under a natural condition on the score distribution, achieves overall optimality. Comparative analysis shows that it matches or exceeds the performance of report‑noisy‑max on all examined score vectors. Moreover, the mechanism is compatible with the sensitivity‑balancing transformation of [10] and can be analyzed under the refined composition framework of [11] with minimal modification. It also extends naturally to the setting of private candidates considered in [12], offering utility gains without requiring bounded sensitivity. Consequently, the permute‑and‑flip mechanism provides a universally applicable, higher‑utility alternative to the exponential mechanism, with immediate practical impact for any differential‑privacy pipeline that relies on private selection.

However, the resulting model is typically effective only for the specific target distribution for which data have been prepared [6]–[13].

The use of unlabeled test data dates back to transductive learning in the 1990s [14]. Vapnik characterized transduction as “trying to get the answer that you really need but not a more general one” [15]. Early transductive methods applied this principle to support‑vector machines by incorporating test instances as additional constraints on the decision‑boundary margin [16]–[18]. A parallel line of work on local learning trained a separate model on the nearest neighbors of each test input before making a prediction [19], [20].

In computer‑vision research, several works have explored continued training at deployment. For example, face detection can be improved by bootstrapping difficult faces from easier ones within the same test image [21]; personalized generative models have been obtained by fine‑tuning on a few images of an individual [22]; super‑resolution networks have been trained from scratch on each test image [23]; and video‑segmentation efficiency has been increased by a student model that learns online from a teacher model on test videos [24].

The approach has been extended to diverse domains, including vision‑based reinforcement learning [26], legged locomotion [27], video object tracking [28], natural‑language question answering [29], and medical imaging [30]. The original TTT method employed rotation prediction as a self‑supervised pretext task, asking the model to classify the angle of a 90°‑multiple rotation [31]. This task can be overly easy for natural outdoor scenes—where horizon orientation suffices—or overly hard for top‑down views where many orientations appear equally plausible.

[ANSWER]: Traditional graph tasks such as link prediction [1], knowledge base completion [2], and basic one‑hop query answering are essentially variants of a single‑variable inference problem: determining whether a triple (h, r, t) exists in a knowledge graph (KG) or whether an entity t satisfies a query of the form (h, r, ?). These tasks assume that only one element of the triple is missing.  

Knowledge graph reasoning extends this setting to queries that may involve multiple missing edges or nodes in large, incomplete KGs. Such queries can be expressed as path queries, conjunctive queries, disjunctive queries, or combinations thereof, and require inference over multiple hops and logical operators. Formal treatments of KG reasoning define a KG as a set of entities 𝔈, a set of relations ℛ, and a set of triples 𝔗 ⊆ 𝔈 × ℛ × 𝔈, with reasoning tasks aiming to predict triples absent from the original graph 𝔗 [3].  

Embedding‑based approaches have been proposed to answer multi‑hop queries on KGs. Methods such as those in [4]–[7] learn vector representations that support traversal and composition over several hops, enabling the answering of conjunctive and path‑based queries. Related work on question answering over KGs also leverages embeddings to map natural‑language questions to logical forms that can be executed on the graph [8, 9].  

Beyond embeddings, a variety of techniques address KG reasoning. Attention mechanisms have been employed to weight relevant parts of the graph during inference [11]. Reinforcement‑learning frameworks treat query answering as a sequential decision process, training agents to navigate the graph toward answers; notable examples include the approaches in [10, 12] and the DIVA model [13]. Neural logic networks integrate logical operators directly into neural architectures, learning to approximate logical inference through differentiable modules [14, 15].  

Collectively, these lines of work explore different aspects of KG reasoning, ranging from representation learning and neural operator design to search‑based and logic‑guided inference strategies.

[ANSWER]: Structure learning for Bayesian networks has long been recognized as an NP‑hard problem, motivating two principal families of methods.  Constraint‑based approaches infer conditional independences from data and then search for a DAG that is consistent with those independences.  Score‑based methods assign a numerical score reflecting goodness‑of‑fit—often combined with a complexity penalty—to each candidate DAG and then search the combinatorial space for a high‑scoring structure.  Over the years, a variety of scoring functions have been proposed, each incorporating either an implicit or explicit regularization term to avoid overfitting.  Approximate algorithms with probabilistic guarantees have been developed to produce high‑scoring graphs despite the exponential size of the search space, while exact algorithms exploit structural restrictions such as a bound on the number of parents per node, extending classic results like the Chow‑Liu tree construction to more general settings.  Sampling techniques that operate over node orderings rather than directly over DAGs have also been introduced, and once a graph structure is fixed, a range of methods exist for estimating edge weights, including scenarios with latent variables.

Continuous‑relaxation approaches address the difficulty of directly optimizing over discrete DAGs by embedding the adjacency matrix in a continuous space and enforcing acyclicity through differentiable penalties.  Early work formulated the problem as a least‑squares fit of a linear‑Gaussian structural equation model, augmenting the loss with a term that vanishes only when the relaxed matrix corresponds to an acyclic graph.  Subsequent contributions have refined the acyclicity penalty, proposing alternatives that improve optimization stability and convergence.  The GOLEM framework specifically targets linear‑Gaussian SEMs, showing that the squared loss aligns with the log‑likelihood and that a suitably designed penalty can replace the augmented‑Lagrangian scheme of earlier methods, enabling more efficient gradient‑based optimization over the relaxed adjacency matrix.

Learning a suitable ordering of variables is closely related to structure discovery in SEMs, as a DAG can be represented by a permutation of nodes together with a lower‑triangular weight matrix.  Autoregressive models illustrate this connection: the value of a variable depends on its predecessors in a given ordering, and certain permutations yield higher likelihoods.  Methods for discovering beneficial orderings have therefore been explored, ranging from heuristic searches to algorithms that treat the permutation as a latent variable.  Recent approaches employ continuous relaxations of permutations to enable gradient‑based learning; however, earlier latent‑permutation models relied on hard assignments and the REINFORCE estimator, which suffers from high variance compared with reparameterized gradient techniques.

Bayesian causal discovery seeks a full posterior distribution over DAGs rather than a single point estimate, offering a principled quantification of uncertainty.  Classical Bayesian methods, often based on exact or Monte‑Carlo inference, encounter scalability limits in high‑dimensional settings, prompting the development of approximate schemes such as Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational approximations.  While these approaches improve tractability, challenges remain in representing the discrete, combinatorial nature of graph structures and in achieving low‑variance stochastic optimization.

Continuous relaxations of permutations are employed to obtain reparameterized, low‑variance gradient estimators, while a horseshoe prior on edge weights encourages sparsity.  By integrating these design choices, the approach scales to high‑dimensional problems, quantifies uncertainty in the inferred graph, and achieves superior performance on standard causal‑discovery benchmarks—particularly in low‑sample regimes—relative to existing maximum‑likelihood and Bayesian baselines.

The third sub‑category exploits ensembles of classifiers to achieve fairness. By aggregating the outputs of several models—often trained with diverse fairness constraints—or by selecting a subset of models that together satisfy a fairness criterion, these approaches aim to inherit the strengths of each constituent predictor [11]. [ANSWER]: Robust classification has been extensively studied, and the majority of approaches assume a uniform robustness radius that applies to every input.  Early and influential works on adversarial attacks and defenses—including those by Szegedy et al., Goodfellow et al., Carlini & Wagner, Madry et al., and many subsequent papers—focus on neural‑network models and enforce norm‑ball constraints (typically ℓ₂ or ℓ∞) of a fixed size around each example.  These methods analyze the trade‑off between accuracy and robustness under the assumption that the same perturbation budget is relevant for all regions of the data distribution.

A line of research has explored the possibility of using input‑dependent robustness budgets.  Methods such as those proposed by Zhang et al. and Wang et al. train neural networks with varying radii across examples, trading off robustness and accuracy in a data‑dependent manner.  While these approaches relax the uniform‑radius assumption, they remain centered on neural‑network architectures, retain norm‑ball perturbation sets, and are primarily evaluated empirically rather than through a unified theoretical framework.

Connections between robustness and large‑margin classification have also been investigated.  The support‑vector machine (SVM) and its variants constitute the classic large‑margin linear classifier, seeking to maximize the minimal distance between training points and the decision boundary.  More recent works have extended large‑margin ideas to nonlinear settings, for example by constructing Lipschitz‑constrained classifiers, by optimizing worst‑case margins for deep networks, or by learning metric embeddings that yield large‑margin nearest‑neighbor classifiers.  These studies aim to increase the global margin of a model, whereas the robustness literature often focuses on ensuring a fixed perturbation radius rather than adapting the margin locally.

Robustness of non‑parametric classifiers has been examined both from an attack and a defense perspective.  Several papers have demonstrated that nearest‑neighbor, kernel, and histogram methods are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations.  Defensive strategies include adversarial pruning of the training set to improve 1‑NN robustness (Wang et al.) and the development of the so‑called “max‑astute” classifier, which maximizes accuracy on points that are robust under a prescribed radius (Yang et al.).  These works highlight the challenges of achieving both high accuracy and adversarial robustness with instance‑based methods.

Theoretical analyses of weight‑function‑based estimators have provided conditions under which such non‑parametric methods converge to optimal classifiers in the large‑sample limit.  Stone’s classic results and subsequent extensions establish that, for distributions with a positive separation margin between classes, k‑nearest‑neighbor and kernel estimators satisfy consistency requirements.  More recent studies have shown that, after preprocessing steps such as adversarial pruning to enforce class separation, these estimators can achieve both robustness and accuracy asymptotically.  These analyses differ in the target optimality notion and in the technical assumptions required for convergence.

Concurrent research has introduced a related limiting classifier termed the “margin‑canonical Bayes” classifier.  That line of work focuses on a data‑augmentation scheme designed to guarantee convergence of certain algorithms to this limit, emphasizing algorithmic modifications rather than the intrinsic properties of classical non‑parametric estimators.

In this paper we introduce the neighborhood‑preserving Bayes optimal classifier, a new large‑sample limit that extends the Bayes optimal decision rule beyond the support of the data by labeling each out‑of‑support point with the class of its nearest in‑support neighbor.  This construction yields maximal robustness regions while preserving Bayes‑optimal accuracy, thereby eliminating the traditional robustness‑accuracy trade‑off.  We formulate sufficient conditions under which weight‑function estimators converge to this limit, and we prove that k‑nearest‑neighbor classifiers satisfy these conditions when the number of neighbors grows sub‑linearly with the sample size, and that kernel classifiers converge provided the kernel has faster‑than‑polynomial decay and the bandwidth shrinks sufficiently slowly. Together, these results provide a comprehensive theoretical foundation for achieving locally adaptive robustness with classical non‑parametric methods, and they clarify the relationship between existing robust‑optimal notions and the proposed neighborhood‑preserving formulation.

[ANSWER]: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) were introduced as a non‑cooperative two‑player game in which a generator attempts to produce samples that a discriminator cannot distinguish from real data [1]. The discriminator outputs the probability that its input originates from the data distribution, while the generator seeks to make this discrimination difficult. This formulation leads to a saddle‑point objective that can be interpreted as minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the data and model distributions. Numerous variants have been proposed to improve training stability and mitigate mode collapse, employing alternative divergences and distance measures [2]–[13].

Co‑generation concerns generating a subset of an output space conditioned on the complementary subset, a setting that appears in tasks such as image inpainting [14],[15] and image‑to‑image translation [16]–[23]. Conditional GANs generate entire outputs from an input signal [24],[25], but typically do not decompose the output into arbitrary subsets. Multi‑modal Boltzmann machines learn shared representations across modalities such as video‑audio [27] or image‑text [26], and encoder‑decoder architectures based on restricted Boltzmann machines reconstruct one modality from another. Deep joint‑embedding approaches map images and text to a common vector space, enabling manipulation in the embedding space followed by decoding [28]. Cross‑domain image generation methods employ encoder‑decoder networks to transfer attributes like rotation, translation, or style between objects [29]–[32].

Image‑to‑image translation learns mappings between two domains using either supervised strategies [33]–[37] or unsupervised variants [38]–[43]. Cycle‑consistency regularization [44]–[45] and distance‑preserving constraints [46] have been introduced to improve correspondence between domains. Recent work investigates disentangled representations [17],[18] and addresses inherent ambiguities [23]; alternative loss formulations such as triangle losses have also been explored [47],[48]. Attribute transfer, analogy learning, and a broad range of style‑transfer techniques [49]–[65] adopt encoder‑decoder frameworks that map whole samples from one domain to another, similar to inpainting‑based feature learning [14].

Because many encoder‑decoder approaches require a separate decoder for each possible subset of the output space, they do not scale to arbitrary sub‑space generation without prior knowledge of the subsets of interest. Exceptions that handle partial observations include style‑transfer methods [66], image‑inpainting approaches [15], and coupled generative adversarial nets (CoGANs) [67]. CoGANs learn a joint distribution over multiple domains by coupling generators (and optionally discriminators) through weight sharing, and discuss cross‑domain image transformation and coverage issues [67].

Annealed importance sampling (AIS) is an algorithm originally devised for estimating partition‑function ratios [68]–[70]; by gradually transforming samples from a simple distribution (e.g., a multivariate Gaussian) into samples from a target distribution, AIS can be repurposed to draw accurate samples from complex distributions. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) combines Markov‑chain Monte Carlo with Hamiltonian dynamics, using auxiliary kinetic energy and Metropolis updates along trajectories that preserve the Hamiltonian value [71]–[75]. The reduced random‑walk behavior of HMC makes it well‑suited for sampling in co‑generation settings.

[ANSWER]: Knowledge distillation seeks to construct a compact student model from a larger teacher network by transferring either the teacher’s output predictions or intermediate feature representations. Early approaches focused on direct output matching, while later methods incorporated intermediate activations to enrich the transferred knowledge. A common assumption in most distillation techniques is the availability of the original training data during the student’s training phase. This requirement becomes problematic in scenarios where data privacy, copyright, or logistical constraints limit access to the original dataset. To address this limitation, data‑free knowledge distillation has been explored, wherein synthetic samples are generated to replace the missing real data. Although this line of work enables distillation without any genuine inputs, the quality of the synthesized data often falls short of that of real images, leading to noticeable performance drops for students on complex tasks. An alternative strategy involves leveraging out‑of‑distribution (OOD) samples as a surrogate for the original data. However, naïve application of distillation on OOD data typically fails to produce students that match the performance of their teachers, highlighting the difficulty of extracting useful supervisory signals from such samples.

The broader challenge of distribution shift between training and testing data has motivated research in domain adaptation and domain generalization. Traditional learning algorithms generally presume that source (training) and target (testing) data share the same underlying distribution, an assumption frequently violated in practice. Domain adaptation methods aim to reduce the discrepancy between source and target domains, often by aligning feature spaces or employing adversarial objectives, and usually require access to unlabeled target data during training. Recent extensions have considered open‑set settings where the label spaces differ between domains. In contrast, domain generalization seeks to learn models that perform well on unseen target domains without any exposure to target data during training, typically by exploiting multiple source domains or by enforcing invariance to domain‑specific cues. While both adaptation and generalization have achieved notable success in supervised learning contexts, their intersection with knowledge distillation remains relatively under‑explored, particularly under OOD conditions.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) introduced a powerful framework for image synthesis by training a generator to deceive a discriminator in a minimax game. Subsequent research has focused on improving GAN performance along several dimensions: enhancing image quality, increasing diversity of generated samples, and stabilizing the training dynamics. Additional efforts have explored data‑efficient GAN training through transfer learning and data augmentation techniques, enabling high‑fidelity generation from limited datasets. When the original training data are unavailable, conventional GAN training becomes infeasible, prompting investigations into alternative synthesis strategies suitable for OOD settings.

The sparsity patterns encountered in practice differ markedly depending on the acquisition method. LiDAR sensors generate structured sparsity that reflects the scanning geometry of the device. Feature‑based SLAM systems such as ORB‑SLAM produce depth only at detected feature locations. In many of these designs the two branches extract features independently and later fuse them through concatenation, addition, or by using RGB features to guide refinement of the depth prediction. Such approaches work well on benchmarks where the sparsity is moderate, but they may struggle when the depth measurements are extremely sparse.

Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a classical statistical technique for finding a shared subspace in which representations from two modalities are maximally correlated. To overcome the linearity constraint of traditional CCA, Deep CCA (DCCA) introduced nonlinear projections learned by deep neural networks, enabling more expressive cross‑modal mappings. A common alternative to the standard average loss in empirical risk minimization is to replace the simple mean with a min‑max objective that seeks to minimize the maximum loss. Such min‑max formulations have been employed for a variety of purposes, including ensuring fairness across subgroups, enhancing robustness to adversarial perturbations, and improving generalization to unseen domains. Smooth approximations to the max, often realized via LogSumExp or exponential smoothing operators, provide differentiable surrogates that retain the desirable worst‑case properties while enabling efficient optimization. These approximations appear in geometric programming, boosting, and recent neural network architectures that interpolate between sum and max operations. Connections between smooth aggregation and superquantile (conditional value‑at‑risk) methods have also been explored, allowing practitioners to target specific quantiles of the loss distribution by tuning a smoothing parameter.

In robust regression, losses such as the Huber loss, Tukey’s biweight, and more general M‑estimators are widely used to mitigate the influence of outliers. Exponentially tilted losses have been investigated for squared‑error regression, yielding formulations that correspond to specific risk measures. Other strategies suppress large losses by favoring small residuals or applying gradient clipping, whereas the opposite extreme magnifies hard examples to focus learning on difficult samples, a principle that underlies several curriculum‑learning and hard‑example‑mining techniques. Fairness constraints have also been incorporated directly into loss design, encouraging equitable performance across protected groups. These approaches typically treat robustness and fairness as separate design goals, requiring distinct loss modifications for each.

[ANSWER]: Knowledge distillation was introduced by Hinton et al., who transferred the “dark knowledge” of a high‑capacity teacher to a compact student by minimizing the Kullback‑Leibler divergence between their softened output distributions. Since then, a multitude of extensions have been proposed, including FitNets, attention transfer, CCM, FSP, SP, CCKD, and various task‑specific KD formulations, all aimed at improving the fidelity of the transferred knowledge. A common design choice in these works is to employ a well‑trained, high‑performing teacher, under the assumption that superior teacher accuracy yields better student performance.

Ensemble learning has been widely combined with knowledge distillation to further enhance generalization. Methods that distill from ensembles of independently trained teachers have reported notable gains, and online distillation frameworks have sought to increase the diversity among multiple models during training, thereby strengthening the ensemble effect. The prevailing view in these approaches remains that stronger ensembles, achieved through longer training or larger model capacities, are preferable for distillation.

A line of research has challenged the notion that the strongest possible teacher is always optimal. Empirical studies have shown that a large capacity gap between teacher and student can impede effective knowledge transfer. To mitigate this gap, several strategies have been explored: introducing an intermediate‑size assistant network, designing “tolerant” teachers via softened loss functions, or constructing student‑friendly teachers by embedding student branches during training. While these works demonstrate that reducing the teacher‑student mismatch can improve distillation, they typically lack a unifying theoretical explanation for the observed gap.

Self‑distillation frameworks provide another perspective by using a model’s own intermediate checkpoints as teachers for its later iterations. These approaches implicitly exploit the potential of intermediate representations, yet most prior studies treat the choice of checkpoint empirically and do not offer a principled analysis of why certain intermediate models may be more effective teachers than fully converged ones.

The information bottleneck (IB) principle, originally formulated by Tishby et al., offers a theoretical lens for understanding the trade‑off between compression of input information and preservation of relevant target information in deep networks. Subsequent work has applied the IB framework to interpret training dynamics, to improve representation learning, and even to guide deep reinforcement learning. However, the connection between IB theory and knowledge distillation has remained largely unexplored.

In contrast, we demonstrate that intermediate checkpoints—despite having lower final accuracy—can serve as superior teachers compared with fully converged models, and that a weak snapshot ensemble of such checkpoints can outperform a strong ensemble of independently trained, fully converged teachers. By linking these empirical findings to the IB principle, we show that intermediate models retain higher mutual information with the input, thereby providing richer “dark knowledge” for the student. Building on this insight, we propose an algorithm that selects the optimal intermediate teacher by maximizing task‑related mutual information while minimizing nuisance information. Extensive experiments across diverse distillation scenarios validate the effectiveness of the proposed selection strategy, the superiority of snapshot ensembles, and the overall benefit of viewing KD through the information bottleneck perspective.

[ANSWER]: Deep clustering methods have leveraged the expressive power of neural networks to learn representations and cluster assignments jointly. Early approaches combined reconstruction objectives with clustering loss functions, while later works incorporated pairwise relationships, multi‑task learning, or other auxiliary signals. These joint frameworks typically optimize a weighted sum of several losses, which can be difficult to balance in practice when validation data are scarce, leading to sensitivity to hyper‑parameter choices.

Probabilistic deep clustering has been explored from both generative and discriminative perspectives. Generative models introduce latent variables and impose mixture‑of‑Gaussians priors on latent representations to model the data‑generation process. Although such assumptions can capture certain statistical regularities, they may be violated for complex visual data and do not always translate into superior clustering performance. Discriminative probabilistic methods, by contrast, model the direct mapping from inputs to cluster labels and often maximize mutual information, achieving higher cluster accuracy. However, these approaches tend to ignore instance‑specific details that could enhance representation learning and consequently benefit clustering.

Several recent works have combined the mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) paradigm with deep clustering. Methods such as MIXAE, DAMIC, and MoE‑Sim‑VAE integrate MoE with reconstruction‑based objectives, but they rely on additional mechanisms such as pre‑training stages, regularization terms, or auxiliary clustering losses to achieve good performance. These extra components increase algorithmic complexity and may limit scalability.

Contrastive learning has become a dominant paradigm for learning discriminative visual representations without labels. A variety of contrastive objectives have been proposed, ranging from instance discrimination with noise‑contrastive estimation to pretext tasks such as colorization and context auto‑encoding. Architectures like InstDisc, MoCo, and related extensions maintain memory banks or momentum encoders to compute efficient contrastive losses. While the resulting embeddings excel on downstream tasks after fine‑tuning, most contrastive frameworks are not directly optimized for clustering. Some recent attempts, such as PCL, augment contrastive learning with an auxiliary clustering objective (e.g., k‑means) to expose semantic structure, but they still require extra clustering steps and focus on learning transferable embeddings rather than discovering intrinsic data groups.

By employing a gating network to assign data points to expert modules and training each expert with a contrastive objective, the method captures both fine‑grained instance discrimination and high‑level semantic partitioning within a single objective. A scalable Expectation‑Maximization algorithm is derived to handle the latent variables, with theoretical guarantees on the monotonic improvement and convergence of the evidence lower bound. Unlike prior MoE‑based clustering approaches, the proposed method does not rely on pre‑training, explicit regularization, or separate clustering losses. Compared with purely discriminative or generative probabilistic models, it preserves instance‑level detail while modeling cluster semantics. Extensive experiments on four widely used natural‑image benchmarks demonstrate that the approach consistently outperforms strong contrastive baselines and a broad range of existing deep clustering methods, establishing a new state‑of‑the‑art for unsupervised image clustering.

Incorporating explicit budget constraints into pruning has also been explored. Variational‑based approaches enforce budget constraints during pruning, but may need additional safeguards—such as ensuring at least one active channel in down‑sampling layers—to remain stable under very low‑resource budgets.

In this setting, two broad families of queries are distinguished. Conditional probability queries ask for the probability of a subset of variables given observed values of another subset, requiring marginalization over the remaining variables. Assignment queries, also known as most probable explanation (MPE) or maximum a posteriori (MAP) queries when no evidence variables are present, seek the highest‑probability assignment to a set of variables conditioned on observed evidence. Foundational works on these problems established the theoretical underpinnings and algorithmic approaches for both exact and approximate inference.

When the underlying model exhibits a sparse Markov dependence structure, a substantial body of work has leveraged this property to obtain efficient inference algorithms. In sequential settings, recursive computation techniques such as the forward‑backward algorithm and dynamic programming exploit the limited connectivity of Markov chains or hidden Markov models, enabling tractable evaluation of both conditional and assignment queries. However, autoregressive neural sequence models differ fundamentally from traditional Markovian models: their hidden state is a continuous vector that summarizes the entire history, producing a combinatorial tree of exponentially many future trajectories. Consequently, classic dynamic‑programming methods do not apply, and both conditional probability and assignment queries become computationally intractable in the worst case, with NP‑hardness results documented for related inference problems.

In natural language processing and related domains, a considerable literature has addressed assignment‑type queries for neural sequence models, focusing on the MAP problem of generating high‑quality sequences conditioned on a prefix or auxiliary context. Heuristic decoding strategies such as beam search, best‑first search, various sampling schemes, and hybrid approaches have been proposed and empirically validated for producing plausible outputs. These methods are primarily designed to approximate the most likely sequence rather than to estimate arbitrary conditional probabilities. While some decoding techniques can be repurposed to obtain lower‑bound estimates of probabilities, they inherently produce biased estimators and do not provide general solutions for the broader class of conditional probability queries.

Because the decoder treats the output as a sequence, it suffers from the “responsibility problem”: the loss landscape becomes discontinuous with respect to permutations of the target set, leading to unstable training. Some point‑cloud methods mitigate this issue by imposing domain‑specific assumptions, such as treating points as independent samples or arranging them on a regular grid, but these constraints limit applicability to more general set‑structured data.

A second line of work replaces the MLP with a recurrent neural network (RNN) decoder that generates set elements sequentially. When a canonical ordering can be defined—often by exploiting domain knowledge such as a breadth‑first traversal of a graph—this approach sidesteps the permutation issue. However, the requirement of a predefined order restricts the method to settings where such an ordering is natural or easy to compute, and it does not fully address the underlying set‑symmetry.

Iterative optimization‑based models constitute a closely related family. Mordatch introduced a framework that minimizes an energy function inside each forward pass and differentiates through the optimization loop. Their experiments demonstrated the ability to modify small 2‑D point sets, but the scalability of this approach to larger, more complex tasks such as object detection remains uncertain. The energy‑based formulation differs from direct set‑distance minimization, making it less transparent how the predicted set aligns with the target.

Auto‑encoding architectures that pool a set into a single feature vector and share this representation with a decoder have also been explored. By designing a permutation‑equivariant decoder, these models avoid the responsibility problem within an auto‑encoder setting. However, because inference requires an encoder to supply the pooled representation, they are unsuitable for direct set prediction where only a feature vector is available at test time. Early large‑scale collections such as ImageNet demonstrated that growing data volume can simultaneously introduce subtle correlations, for example background cues that leak object class information. Subsequent crowd‑sourced resources amplified this issue, as annotators inject uncontrolled socio‑economic signals that become entangled with the target labels. In visual question answering, analyses revealed that questions alone often suffice to predict correct answers, prompting re‑annotation efforts and revised train‑test splits to mitigate language‑only shortcuts. Similar observations were made for audio‑visual scene‑aware dialog, where the textual query can dominate over visual and acoustic streams, and for natural language inference datasets where lexical heuristics correlate with labels. Story‑completion corpora have also been shown to admit length‑based predictors that bypass narrative understanding. More recently, the SocialIQ benchmark, intended for social‑situational reasoning, was found to be solvable with text alone because sentiment cues strongly align with the correct statements, highlighting the persistence of modality‑specific biases across diverse tasks.

A variety of techniques have been proposed to reduce or compensate for such dataset biases. Approaches that target known biased attributes—such as gender in vision—often mask or remove the corresponding visual regions, or explicitly re‑balance training distributions using test‑set statistics. In the context of visual question answering, several methods train an auxiliary classifier on the question modality and use its predictions to regularize the main model, either by masking softmax outputs, employing product‑of‑experts formulations, or jointly optimizing a full model together with a question‑only expert. These strategies share the reliance on a subset classifier to expose and attenuate the influence of biased cues. While effective at limiting shortcut learning, they differ from methods that evaluate bias by directly perturbing input modalities after training.

Feature‑importance and interpretability techniques provide complementary insights into model behavior at the level of individual inputs. Local surrogate models such as LIME approximate a linear explanation around a specific instance, whereas DeepLIFT and SHAP compute attribution scores based on back‑propagation or Shapley value approximations, respectively. Extensions that combine DeepLIFT with Shapley theory (Deep SHAP) further refine these estimates. Other work investigates cross‑modal interactions by approximating a multimodal predictor with a set of single‑modality models, thereby quantifying the benefit of modality fusion. These methods focus on fine‑grained feature contributions, whereas the emerging need is for metrics that assess the reliance on an entire modality in a unified and model‑agnostic manner.

In this work we introduce a simple, model‑agnostic metric—the perceptual score—that quantifies how much a multimodal classifier depends on each input modality. We apply this metric to a broad collection of visual question answering and visual dialog models across several benchmark datasets, uncovering a consistent trend in which newer, higher‑accuracy models rely increasingly on textual cues while neglecting visual input. The perceptual score also enables a fine‑grained bias analysis by decomposing the overall reliance into contributions from specific data subsets, such as question types. [ANSWER]: Existing kernels that enable linear‑time Gaussian process (GP) regression on unstructured data are typically based on inducing points, which are closely related to Nyström approximations. For a set of inducing locations \(Z\) and a base kernel \(k\), the inducing‑point kernel can be written as \(k_{\text{IP}}(x,x') = k(x,Z)K_{ZZ}^{-1}k(Z,x')\), where \(K_{ZZ}\) is the kernel matrix on the inducing set. Variants of this construction differ in the way the inducing points are selected or in the regularisation applied to \(K_{ZZ}\), but all share the property that the resulting kernel matrix is low‑rank, yielding computational savings.

Sparse Gaussian Process Regression (SGPR) builds on the inducing‑point idea by selecting a subset of \(m\) inducing points and approximating the full kernel matrix with a low‑rank plus diagonal correction. The predictive mean and covariance admit compact expressions that involve the inverse of a small \(m\times m\) matrix and the observation noise variance. This formulation leads to \(\mathcal{O}(nm^{2})\) training cost and \(\mathcal{O}(nm)\) prediction cost, which are linear in the number of data points when \(m\) is held fixed. However, the dimensionality of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) induced by an SGPR kernel is limited by the number of inducing points, restricting model expressivity.

Sparse variational GP (SVGP) methods formulate GP inference as a variational optimisation problem in which the variational distribution is defined over a set of inducing points. The resulting kernel incorporates both the prior covariance and the variational parameters, and its low‑rank structure again provides \(\mathcal{O}(nm^{2})\) training complexity. While SVGP can accommodate non‑zero prior means and offers principled uncertainty quantification, its RKHS dimensionality remains bounded by the number of inducing points, and the variational optimisation introduces additional computational overhead.

Inducing‑frequency kernels constitute another family of scalable GP approximations. By projecting the kernel onto a set of spectral features or random Fourier bases, these methods replace the original kernel with a finite‑dimensional approximation that can be evaluated in linear time. Approaches based on random Fourier features or structured spectral approximations achieve \(\mathcal{O}(n)\) or \(\mathcal{O}(n\log n)\) computational cost, but they are most effective for low‑dimensional data and may suffer from reduced fidelity when the true kernel exhibits complex, non‑stationary structure.

Tree‑based kernel constructions have been explored for specific data modalities. Earlier work introduced kernels defined over points residing on the leaves of a single tree or on multiple trees, where the kernel value depends on the depth of the deepest common ancestor. Although conceptually appealing, those methods required \(\mathcal{O}(n^{2})\) time to construct and invert the kernel matrix, limiting their applicability to large datasets. Recent advances in structured kernels for ordered or hierarchical data exploit Toeplitz or Kronecker algebra to achieve \(\mathcal{O}(n\log n)\) or even \(\mathcal{O}(n)\) time for one‑dimensional or grid‑structured inputs, but such techniques rely on strong assumptions about the data layout.

Iterative linear‑system solvers, notably conjugate‑gradient (CG) methods, have been employed to avoid explicit matrix inversion in GP inference. Instruction‑following corpora in natural‑language processing similarly introduce train‑test splits that isolate distinct generalisation challenges, while the Abstract Reasoning Corpus (ARC) measures extrapolation of geometric patterns without involving sequential decision making. Beyond benchmark design, a variety of algorithmic approaches have been proposed to improve robustness in imitation learning.  Meta‑imitation learning and meta‑IRL methods assume access to a large collection of demonstrations for a set of training tasks and aim to adapt quickly to new test tasks with only a few demonstrations.  Such approaches leverage shared structure across tasks to enable knowledge transfer, and they have been shown effective in multi‑task settings where train and test distributions are relatively similar.  Multi‑task and multi‑modal imitation learning techniques also seek to reduce over‑fitting by exposing agents to diverse demonstration conditions, employing data augmentation, or altering observation viewpoints.  However, these methods typically presuppose that the underlying objectives remain consistent across train and test settings, and they provide limited guarantees when the test environment differs substantially in dynamics, visual appearance, or object composition.

In this work we introduce a comprehensive benchmark suite for robust imitation learning that directly addresses the gaps identified in prior literature.  The suite defines a unified 2‑D universe containing a robot manipulator and a configurable set of objects, and it provides a fixed demonstration variant for each task together with multiple systematically varied test variants that independently modify object colour, shape, count, dynamics, and camera perspective.  By separating demonstration and execution environments and by varying several semantically meaningful axes, the benchmark enables precise measurement of an algorithm’s ability to generalise demonstrator intent rather than merely reproducing observed behaviour. Using this benchmark we demonstrate that contemporary imitation‑learning algorithms over‑fit to the training context and that standard robustness‑enhancing techniques—such as multitask training, data augmentation, and alternative viewpoints—yield only modest improvements, especially under large distribution shifts. Early works such as BinaryConnect [4] and Ternary‑Weight Networks [5] focus on aggressively quantizing the weight tensors while keeping activations in full precision. These approaches demonstrate impressive memory savings but typically incur a noticeable drop in top‑1 accuracy (e.g., a 5 % loss on ImageNet [1]). More recent fine‑grained methods [6, 7] improve accuracy by applying per‑layer or per‑filter ternary quantization, yet they rely on post‑training fine‑tuning and are not suited for training networks from scratch. Our work departs from this line by jointly reducing the precision of both weights and activations during training, and compensating the potential accuracy loss through a systematic increase in network width, thereby preserving or surpassing the baseline performance without requiring a fine‑tuning stage.

A second strand of literature targets activation quantization, often in conjunction with weight quantization, to obtain end‑to‑end low‑precision pipelines. By contrast, we demonstrate that a modest 4‑bit activation precision combined with a 2‑bit weight representation can match full‑precision accuracy when the network is made wider, and that even binary activations become viable when the width is appropriately scaled. [ANSWER]: The use of a cache of past events to guide decision making has a long history across several fields. Early approaches framed this idea as case‑based reasoning, where a new problem is solved by adapting solutions from similar previously encountered cases [1]. In reinforcement learning, non‑parametric methods and episodic memory mechanisms have been proposed to retrieve and reuse experience [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Some of these works focus on augmenting an agent’s working memory within a single episode [8, 9] or across a short sequence of related episodes [10], while others aim to exploit a broader, persistent knowledge base that can span multiple episodes and even incorporate information from other agents.

A number of prior methods prescribe a fixed way of integrating retrieved information into the decision‑making process. For instance, several approaches define the action‑value function directly in terms of value estimates previously generated for similar states [11, 12, 13, 14], or they construct a model of the environment from observed transitions and use this model for planning [15]. By hard‑coding the relationship between retrieved data and the agent’s predictions, these techniques limit the flexibility with which the agent can learn to combine parametric computation and external memory.

More recent work has introduced attention mechanisms to select relevant portions of a retrieval set. One notable example learns to attend over a small batch of trajectories sampled from a dataset, thereby determining which past experiences should influence the current prediction [16]. However, the scale of the retrieval set in such methods remains limited, and they do not exploit the full breadth of available experience.

Experience‑replay techniques constitute another major class of methods that leverage a stored transition dataset. By repeatedly sampling past experiences during training, replay buffers enable agents to perform additional gradient updates per observed transition [17, 18, 19, 20]. While this improves sample efficiency during learning, the replayed data does not directly affect the agent’s behaviour at test time, requires further learning steps to incorporate new information, and does not provide an end‑to‑end mechanism for relating past experience to novel situations.

In contrast, the present work introduces a semi‑parametric architecture that combines fast approximate nearest‑neighbor retrieval with end‑to‑end learning, allowing an agent to attend to tens of millions of expert demonstrations during inference. By integrating large‑scale retrieval into an offline reinforcement‑learning setting for 9×9 Go, the approach demonstrates substantial gains in prediction accuracy and gameplay performance over strong non‑retrieval baselines. The method further enables updates to the knowledge base at evaluation time without additional training, and shows that incorporating new game data can improve performance on the fly, highlighting the benefits of scalable, flexible retrieval‑augmented decision making.

[ANSWER]: Sample weighting has long been used to mitigate biased training data, beginning with early resampling and instance‑reweighting techniques that rely on prior knowledge to assign fixed weights before learning.  More recent works replace static preprocessing with dynamically updated weighting functions that map a sample’s training loss to its weight, allowing the model to adapt during training.  The majority of these methods fall into two families: monotonically increasing functions that emphasize high‑loss (hard) examples—such as AdaBoost, hard‑example mining, and focal loss—and monotonically decreasing functions that privilege low‑loss (easy) examples—such as self‑paced learning, its many extensions, and iterative re‑weighting schemes.  While effective in specific scenarios (class‑imbalance or noisy labels, respectively), all of them require the practitioner to hand‑craft the functional form and to tune associated hyper‑parameters, limiting their applicability in real‑world settings where data bias is complex or unknown.  In contrast, our approach automatically discovers an explicit weighting function directly from data, eliminating the need for manual design and hyper‑parameter selection while retaining the expressive power to emulate both increasing and decreasing behaviours as needed.  

Meta‑learning has been leveraged to automate the design of weighting schemes.  Methods such as Feature‑Weighted Loss (FWL), “learning to teach”, and MentorNet employ auxiliary networks (e.g., Bayesian approximators, attention‑based DNNs, or bidirectional LSTMs) that ingest rich information—including sample features and gradients—to produce sample weights.  Although these meta‑learners are powerful, their reliance on high‑dimensional inputs and complex architectures makes them difficult to reproduce, to interpret, and to guarantee the preservation of desirable properties (e.g., monotonicity) exhibited by classic weighting functions.  Our method follows the meta‑learning paradigm but deliberately restricts the weight‑net to a single‑hidden‑layer MLP that takes only the scalar loss as input.  This design yields an explicit, easily visualized weighting function, preserves the universality of approximation, and simplifies training and deployment for practitioners.  

A closely related line of work is L2RW, which also uses a meta‑learning loop to adjust sample weights.  The key distinction is that L2RW learns weights implicitly as latent variables without ever materializing an explicit mapping from loss to weight.  This implicitness can cause unstable weight dynamics during training and hampers the transfer of the learned weighting behavior to new tasks.  By contrast, our Meta‑Weight‑Net learns a concrete, parametric function that is both stable (as demonstrated empirically) and readily transferable across related problems, thereby addressing the generalization limitation of implicit approaches.  

Beyond weighting‑based strategies, many methods tackle class imbalance through knowledge transfer or metric learning.  Approaches that transfer representations from majority to minority classes, as well as metric‑learning losses such as triple‑head loss and range loss, have shown promise in exploiting long‑tailed distributions.  However, these techniques operate orthogonally to sample re‑weighting and often require additional architectural modifications or specialized loss designs.  Our contribution complements these lines of work: the learned weighting function can be combined with any backbone network, including those employing transfer or metric‑learning components, to further enhance performance on imbalanced data without altering the underlying model.  

Similarly, a rich literature addresses noisy labels by explicitly correcting or estimating true labels through auxiliary networks, loss‑correction schemes, or co‑training strategies (e.g., GLC, Reed, D2L, S‑Model).  While effective, such methods introduce extra inference steps or auxiliary parameters and typically assume a particular noise model.  In contrast, our method does not attempt to relabel data; instead, it attenuates the influence of potentially corrupted samples by learning a loss‑dependent weight.  This makes the approach agnostic to the specific noise distribution, reduces computational overhead, and can be seamlessly integrated with existing label‑correction pipelines when desired.

Existing methods can be broadly grouped into four families according to how they exploit a learned dynamics model: (i) Dyna‑style algorithms that generate imaginary transitions and combine them with real experience to train a policy with off‑the‑shelf model‑free techniques; (ii) shooting methods that employ model predictive control to plan actions directly; (iii) analytic‑gradient approaches that back‑propagate through the model for policy search; and (iv) model‑augmented value‑expansion methods that use short model rollouts to refine temporal‑difference targets. Our work concentrates on the first family, where the interplay between model learning, imaginary‑data generation, and policy optimization creates a rich set of hyperparameters that must be scheduled throughout training. By focusing on this category, we are able to address the specific gap in theoretical understanding and automated scheduling of the real‑data ratio—a factor that prior work has treated only heuristically.

Within Dyna‑style MBRL, many studies have proposed improvements to individual components. Deep ensembles have become a standard technique for robust model learning, short rollout horizons are advocated to limit compounding model error, and uncertainty‑aware sampling schemes have been introduced to select reliable imagined transitions. Some works train the policy exclusively on imagined data, whereas others fix a constant mixture of real and imagined samples or adapt the mixture based on Q‑function uncertainty. Although these contributions advance the stability and performance of Dyna methods, they do not provide a principled way to coordinate multiple hyperparameters—such as model‑training frequency, policy‑training iterations, rollout length, and especially the proportion of real data—throughout the entire learning process. Our contribution lies in filling this void: we derive a theoretical return‑discrepancy bound that reveals why a gradually increasing real‑data ratio is advantageous, and we embed this insight into a joint hyperparameter‑scheduling framework (AutoMBPO) that automatically tunes all relevant knobs in model‑based policy optimization.

In contrast, our method formulates a hyper‑MDP that captures the full training state (including model error, policy performance, and data statistics) and designs a reward based on the actual return of the underlying RL task. By combining this formulation with the theoretical analysis of the real‑data ratio, AutoMBPO not only outperforms prior automatic tuning methods across a suite of continuous‑control benchmarks but also yields hyperparameter schedules that align with the derived theory, thereby offering both empirical gains and deeper insight into the design of Dyna‑style MBRL algorithms.
