[ANSWER]: Sample weighting has long been used to mitigate biased training data, beginning with early resampling and instance‑reweighting techniques that rely on prior knowledge to assign fixed weights before learning.  More recent works replace static preprocessing with dynamically updated weighting functions that map a sample’s training loss to its weight, allowing the model to adapt during training.  The majority of these methods fall into two families: monotonically increasing functions that emphasize high‑loss (hard) examples—such as AdaBoost, hard‑example mining, and focal loss—and monotonically decreasing functions that privilege low‑loss (easy) examples—such as self‑paced learning, its many extensions, and iterative re‑weighting schemes.  While effective in specific scenarios (class‑imbalance or noisy labels, respectively), all of them require the practitioner to hand‑craft the functional form and to tune associated hyper‑parameters, limiting their applicability in real‑world settings where data bias is complex or unknown.  In contrast, our approach automatically discovers an explicit weighting function directly from data, eliminating the need for manual design and hyper‑parameter selection while retaining the expressive power to emulate both increasing and decreasing behaviours as needed.  

Meta‑learning has been leveraged to automate the design of weighting schemes.  Methods such as Feature‑Weighted Loss (FWL), “learning to teach”, and MentorNet employ auxiliary networks (e.g., Bayesian approximators, attention‑based DNNs, or bidirectional LSTMs) that ingest rich information—including sample features and gradients—to produce sample weights.  Although these meta‑learners are powerful, their reliance on high‑dimensional inputs and complex architectures makes them difficult to reproduce, to interpret, and to guarantee the preservation of desirable properties (e.g., monotonicity) exhibited by classic weighting functions.  Our method follows the meta‑learning paradigm but deliberately restricts the weight‑net to a single‑hidden‑layer MLP that takes only the scalar loss as input.  This design yields an explicit, easily visualized weighting function, preserves the universality of approximation, and simplifies training and deployment for practitioners.  

A closely related line of work is L2RW, which also uses a meta‑learning loop to adjust sample weights.  The key distinction is that L2RW learns weights implicitly as latent variables without ever materializing an explicit mapping from loss to weight.  This implicitness can cause unstable weight dynamics during training and hampers the transfer of the learned weighting behavior to new tasks.  By contrast, our Meta‑Weight‑Net learns a concrete, parametric function that is both stable (as demonstrated empirically) and readily transferable across related problems, thereby addressing the generalization limitation of implicit approaches.  

Beyond weighting‑based strategies, many methods tackle class imbalance through knowledge transfer or metric learning.  Approaches that transfer representations from majority to minority classes, as well as metric‑learning losses such as triple‑head loss and range loss, have shown promise in exploiting long‑tailed distributions.  However, these techniques operate orthogonally to sample re‑weighting and often require additional architectural modifications or specialized loss designs.  Our contribution complements these lines of work: the learned weighting function can be combined with any backbone network, including those employing transfer or metric‑learning components, to further enhance performance on imbalanced data without altering the underlying model.  

Similarly, a rich literature addresses noisy labels by explicitly correcting or estimating true labels through auxiliary networks, loss‑correction schemes, or co‑training strategies (e.g., GLC, Reed, D2L, S‑Model). Early works introduced the InfoNCE loss to predict future views of an image [1], and subsequent studies improved its efficiency [2] and leveraged multi‑view positives [3]. To increase the pool of negatives, memory‑bank approaches stored past embeddings as independent categories [4], while later methods mitigated the resulting representation drift by using large batches [5] or a momentum‑updated encoder [6]. Variants that combine pretext‑invariant objectives [7] or decompose contrastive loss into alignment and uniformity terms [8] further refined the formulation. Although these techniques achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance on large backbones (e.g., ResNet‑50), they assume abundant capacity and consequently perform poorly on compact architectures. Our work directly addresses this gap by introducing a self‑supervised distillation framework that enables small networks to inherit the rich similarity structure learned by a large teacher, thereby overcoming the limitations of conventional contrastive objectives on limited‑capacity models.

Knowledge distillation has been extensively explored for compressing supervised models, where a student is trained to mimic a teacher’s logits [9], attention maps [10], or feature‑level distributions [11,12,13]. Extensions such as CRD [14] adapt contrastive objectives for distillation, yet they remain focused on task‑specific fine‑tuning rather than on learning generic, task‑agnostic representations. In natural‑language processing, distillation has been applied during pre‑training to produce compact language models (e.g., DistilBERT [15], TinyBERT [16], MobileBERT [17]), demonstrating that teacher‑guided pre‑training can yield strong, versatile learners. However, analogous efforts for visual representation learning are lacking; existing visual distillation methods either require labeled data or are confined to the downstream fine‑tuning stage. By formulating SEED as a self‑supervised distillation that transfers the teacher’s similarity‑score distribution to a student without any annotations, we extend the benefits of distillation to the pre‑training phase of vision models, filling an important void in the literature.

A few recent studies have begun to recognize the need for better self‑supervised methods tailored to small networks. CompRess [18] highlights the inefficiency of current SSL algorithms on compact models and proposes architectural adjustments, yet it does not incorporate a teacher‑student paradigm. In contrast, SEED leverages a pre‑trained large teacher to provide a dense, instance‑level similarity signal that can be faithfully reproduced by a lightweight student, resulting in dramatic gains (e.g., >25 % absolute improvement on ImageNet linear probing for EfficientNet‑B0). Thus, our contribution is the first to combine self‑supervised learning with knowledge distillation in a task‑agnostic pre‑training setting for visual models, establishing a new baseline for small‑model representation learning and opening a pathway for further research on efficient SSL.

[ANSWER]: Imbalanced classification has long been recognized as a pervasive challenge in real‑world applications, prompting extensive research on techniques that mitigate the adverse effects of skewed class distributions. Early work primarily addressed the quantity‑imbalance problem, where the number of training examples differs across classes, leading to models that favor majority categories. To rebalance datasets, researchers have explored data‑selection strategies such as active learning, which queries informative samples, and various resampling schemes—including oversampling of minority instances and undersampling of majority ones—to construct more balanced training sets. Complementary model‑training approaches have focused on re‑weighting loss contributions of samples according to class frequencies, thereby encouraging the learner to pay greater attention to under‑represented classes.

Beyond generic resampling and re‑weighting, a line of research has investigated instance‑level filtering methods that aim to reduce the negative influence of samples lying near decision boundaries. Techniques such as Tomek links, NearMiss, and One‑Sided Selection identify and remove borderline or noisy instances based on feature‑space similarity measures. While effective for vector‑based data, these methods rely on explicit feature distances, which can be unreliable in graph settings where the relational structure provides richer contextual information and labeled nodes are often scarce.

Graph‑structured data appear in diverse domains—including social networks, financial markets, e‑commerce, healthcare, and transportation—yet they inherit the same quantity‑imbalance difficulties observed in other modalities. To address this, several graph‑specific strategies have been proposed. DR‑GCN introduces class‑conditioned adversarial training together with constraints on the latent distribution of unlabeled nodes. RA‑GCN learns class‑wise sample weights within an adversarial framework, while AdaGCN applies boosting principles to emphasize minority‑class nodes during training. GraphSMOTE extends the classic SMOTE idea to graphs by synthesizing both node features and edges for minority classes. Although these methods adapt conventional imbalance remedies to the graph domain, they continue to focus exclusively on class size disparities and do not consider the impact of nodes’ structural positions within the network.

A complementary strand of work has sought to exploit the topology of graphs to infer node importance or proximity to decision boundaries. Approaches that select anchor nodes and compute distances or diffusion scores aim to locate absolute positions of all nodes relative to these anchors, thereby informing sampling or weighting decisions. However, such anchor‑based techniques often treat all anchors uniformly, disregarding class‑specific information and relying on a fixed set of reference points, which can limit their ability to capture nuanced boundary interactions that arise from the heterogeneous connectivity patterns of labeled nodes.

In light of these gaps, the present study introduces the notion of topology‑imbalance in node representation learning, emphasizing how asymmetric placement of labeled nodes can shift decision boundaries independently of class frequencies. By analyzing the influence‑conflict phenomenon under label propagation, we propose a conflict‑detection metric that quantifies each labeled node’s relative position to class boundaries without requiring external anchors. Building on this metric, we develop a model‑agnostic re‑weighting framework that adaptively adjusts training contributions of individual nodes based on their structural roles, thereby addressing both quantity‑ and topology‑imbalance simultaneously. Comprehensive experiments across multiple imbalance scenarios, datasets, and graph neural network architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed method, while also revealing varying sensitivities of GNN designs to topology‑imbalance—a perspective that offers new criteria for evaluating and selecting graph learning models.

Multi‑fidelity BO leverages cheaper approximations of the objective to accelerate learning, while other approaches address objectives that are integrals of expensive integrands, sums of squared errors, or compositions of an expensive inner function with a known inexpensive outer function. Composite (or nested) functions have also been addressed in the gradient‑based optimization literature. While many approaches assume that a strong teacher is desirable, several studies have questioned this assumption. The capacity gap between a powerful teacher and a small student can impede effective knowledge transfer [16‑19]. Empirical evidence shows that even poorly performing teachers can yield successful distillation outcomes [18, 19]. To mitigate the adverse effects of the capacity gap, methods such as introducing an assistant network [16, 17] or designing student‑friendly teachers [20, 11] have been proposed, though a comprehensive theoretical explanation for the gap remains an open question. Self‑distillation frameworks, in which intermediate models serve as teachers for later stages, have also been investigated, but the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of intermediate teachers have yet to be fully clarified.

The information bottleneck (IB) principle was first formulated by Tishby et al. [23], who presented a tabular method for numerically solving the IB Lagrangian. Tishby and Zaslavsky [24] later proposed interpreting deep learning through the IB framework, and Shwartz‑Ziv and Tishby [25] applied the principle to analyze training dynamics in deep networks. This line of research has inspired a range of studies that leverage the IB perspective to interpret and improve deep neural networks [26‑28], as well as recent applications of the IB principle to deep reinforcement learning [29‑31]. [ANSWER]: Traditional open‑domain QA systems follow a two‑stage retriever‑reader pipeline, in which a single, deterministic retrieval function (sparse or dense) first selects a fixed set of passages and a reader then extracts an answer from those passages.  This formulation treats each candidate passage independently and does not allow the retrieval process to be conditioned on evidence gathered so far.  Consequently, the retrieved set often contains irrelevant material and the pipeline struggles with questions that require multi‑hop reasoning or complex relational inference.  In contrast, our approach departs from this static pipeline by casting the entire QA process as a partially observed Markov decision process.  This formulation enables the model to maintain a belief state over accumulated evidence and to decide, at each step, whether to invoke a retrieval action (choosing among BM25, dense DPR, or hyperlink‑based search) or to produce the final answer, thereby directly addressing the independence and relevance limitations of traditional pipelines.

Iterative methods improve upon the static pipeline by repeatedly reformulating the query and invoking a retrieval function based on previously collected passages.  Existing work either re‑uses the same retrieval function multiple times or follows a pre‑specified sequence of heterogeneous retrieval operations (e.g., alternating between dense and sparse search or traversing a hyperlink graph).  While these fixed strategies have yielded gains on multi‑hop benchmarks, they remain brittle: a single inappropriate retrieval choice can halt progress on questions whose evidence requirements differ across steps.  Our contribution is to replace these hand‑crafted strategies with an adaptive information‑seeking policy learned via imitation learning.  The policy dynamically selects the most suitable retrieval operation for the current belief state and can terminate early by issuing an answer action when sufficient evidence has been gathered.  This adaptability not only improves retrieval and answer quality on both single‑hop (SQuAD Open) and multi‑hop (HotpotQA fullwiki) datasets but also reduces the number of reading steps required at inference time, demonstrating a clear advantage over prior fixed‑strategy iterative approaches.

[ANSWER]: Prior work has recognized that program‑obfuscation transformations can serve as adversarial perturbations for machine‑learning models that operate on source code [1–4]. These studies highlight the feasibility of using renaming, control‑flow flattening, dead‑code insertion, and similar techniques to generate examples that remain semantically equivalent while confusing downstream predictors. However, none of them provide a systematic method for selecting the subset of transformations that maximally degrade a target model. By contrast, our formulation explicitly models both the choice of program locations and the specific transformation to apply, enabling a principled optimization that yields substantially higher attack success rates than the heuristic approaches of the earlier obfuscation literature.

A distinct line of research has cast the generation of adversarial programs as an optimization problem. [5] introduced a stochastic formulation that maximizes the perplexity of an obscurity language model (OLM) through an MCMC search over transformation sequences. Although this approach optimizes the “obfuscation strength” for a language model, it does not address the robustness of downstream program‑analysis models nor does it accommodate multiple transformation types within a unified objective. Our method extends this idea by defining a differentiable loss based on the target task (e.g., program summarization) and by jointly optimizing location and transformation choices, thereby producing perturbations that are directly tailored to the vulnerabilities of the target model rather than to a generic language‑model metric.

Other recent works have focused on a narrower set of syntactic edits. [6] and the HotFlip family [7,8] propose first‑order gradient methods to replace local variables or insert printable strings, while [9] uses a Metropolis‑Hastings sampler to find optimal variable‑name replacements. These approaches improve over random baselines but limit themselves to a single transformation class and consequently cannot exploit the richer space of obfuscations that we consider. Moreover, they do not address the complementary problem of locating the most impactful program sites. In our experiments we show that jointly optimizing sites and transformations yields up to a 52 % improvement over the best of these methods on both Python and Java summarization benchmarks.

Robust‑training strategies have also been explored. [10] train models to abstain when confronted with potentially adversarial inputs, but their transformation space is small and searched greedily, making the approach difficult to scale to tasks that require global program understanding such as summarization. [11] extend this line by employing a min‑max formulation with an inner maximizer that can apply multiple transformations. Nevertheless, their inner maximizer selects transformation types and locations at random, lacking a principled mechanism for jointly optimizing the two decisions. Our contribution fills this gap: we introduce a joint optimization problem that simultaneously determines the optimal locations and the optimal transformation for each location, and we solve it efficiently with first‑order methods augmented by randomized smoothing. This results in a differentiable adversarial‑program generator that not only attains higher attack success rates than the state‑of‑the‑art min‑max approach but also produces models that are more robust when trained adversarially.

Box‑based embeddings model entities and relations as axis‑aligned hyper‑rectangles, supporting hierarchical and inclusion reasoning. Convex‑cone embeddings introduce angular constraints that naturally capture entailment and subsumption hierarchies. Recent advances have also moved beyond Euclidean spaces, employing hyperbolic geometry such as Poincaré embeddings to better represent hierarchical structures, and hyperbolic entailment cones that combine curvature with angular constraints. [ANSWER]: Sequence‑to‑sequence tasks inherently involve a pair of opposite directions—source‑to‑target and target‑to‑source. Early efforts exploited this symmetry by imposing bidirectional constraints on separate encoder‑decoder models, showing modest gains in machine translation. Dual learning frameworks introduced a reinforcement‑learning loop between two distinct directional translators, while partially shared‑parameter approaches let the two models reuse components that perform similar functions. Variational methods have further modeled the two directions jointly through latent language models, but all of these techniques retain two independent simplex networks. Multilingual approaches have also been used to fuse opposite directions within a single model by sharing parameters across languages; however, the shared encoder‑decoder architecture forces the model to allocate limited capacity simultaneously to encoding and decoding, which can limit performance on each direction.

Non‑autoregressive generation has attracted considerable interest as a means to accelerate inference relative to conventional autoregressive seq2seq models. Fully non‑autoregressive translators produce the entire output in a single parallel pass, but this speedup typically comes at the cost of a noticeable drop in translation quality. Semi‑autoregressive and iterative refinement strategies mitigate this degradation by repeatedly updating an initial prediction, striking a balance between speed and accuracy. These lines of work focus primarily on improving the efficiency of a single directional generation process rather than addressing the structural challenges of modeling two directions within one network.

Reversible neural architectures have been explored for a variety of purposes, most notably to enable exact reconstruction of intermediate activations and thereby reduce memory consumption during training. Reversible residual networks (RevNets) introduced the core idea of computing earlier layer activations from later ones, and subsequent extensions adapted this principle to recurrent networks and Transformers for natural‑language tasks. In computer‑vision, reversible generative adversarial networks have been applied to image‑to‑image translation, demonstrating that reversibility can be leveraged for bidirectional mappings. While these works emphasize memory efficiency or generative modeling, they do not directly target the construction of a duplex sequence‑to‑sequence system that can handle forward and backward translations in a unified, homogeneous fashion.

Building on these prior strands, this work introduces a reversible duplex Transformer that unifies source‑to‑target and target‑to‑source translation within a single, parameter‑efficient model. By eliminating the traditional encoder‑decoder split and adopting a fully reversible Transformer backbone, the architecture ensures homogeneous, non‑autoregressive computation for both directions, allowing the model to be flipped at inference time to obtain the reverse translation without additional parameters. The reversible design enables the use of cycle‑consistency objectives to strengthen intermediate representations, while also providing memory‑saving benefits during training. Empirical evaluation on machine‑translation benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed duplex model achieves the first successful reversible translation, surpassing multitask autoregressive baselines by up to 1.3 BLEU and matching or exceeding state‑of‑the‑art non‑autoregressive systems with comparable latency. Consequently, the approach addresses the limitations of previous bidirectional, non‑autoregressive, and reversible methods by delivering a truly duplex seq2seq solution that leverages both directional signals without capacity competition.

[ANSWER]: Interpretation methods for black‑box NLP models have been organized into three broad families. Gradient‑based approaches exploit local derivatives of the model output with respect to input embeddings to assign token importance (e.g., Simonyan et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016). Reference‑based techniques compare the model’s prediction on the original input with that on a baseline or reference point, attributing relevance to the observed change (e.g., Sundararajan et al., 2017; Shrikumar et al., 2017). Perturbation‑based strategies query the model on systematically altered inputs, such as masked or occluded tokens, and infer importance from the resulting output variations (e.g., Zeiler & Fergus, 2014; Ribeiro et al., 2016). These families differ in their reliance on model internals, computational cost, and sensitivity to input modifications.

A parallel line of research has focused on evaluating the quality of post‑hoc explanations. Faithfulness, the degree to which an interpretation reflects the model’s true reasoning, is commonly assessed with removal‑based or occlusion metrics that delete or mask tokens identified as important and measure the impact on model confidence (e.g., DeYoung et al., 2020; Bastings et al., 2020). Other works propose axiomatic criteria, checking whether explanations satisfy desirable theoretical properties (e.g., Sundararajan et al., 2017). Robustness‑oriented studies examine how explanations change under input perturbations, revealing vulnerabilities in existing methods (e.g., Ancona et al., 2018; Ghorbani et al., 2019). Plausibility—alignment with human judgments—has been evaluated through human subject studies or by testing whether explanations aid downstream tasks or student models (e.g., Hase et al., 2020; Doshi‑Velez & Kim, 2017). Several surveys combine multiple diagnostics to assess both faithfulness and plausibility, while others explicitly argue for separating the two dimensions (e.g., Zhou et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022).

Building on these strands, this work introduces two previously under‑explored notions of faithfulness for NLP explanations: sensitivity, which measures how model predictions react to small adversarial perturbations of tokens highlighted by an interpretation, and stability, which requires consistent explanations for semantically similar inputs. We systematically evaluate a wide range of existing interpretation techniques—including gradient‑based, reference‑based, perturbation‑based, and removal‑based methods—under these new criteria as well as traditional faithfulness metrics. Guided by the sensitivity notion, we develop a family of robustness‑based interpretation methods that leverage adversarial attack and certification techniques from the robustness literature, demonstrating superior performance on both sensitivity and stability while mitigating gradient saturation issues observed in removal‑based evaluations. Finally, we extend the evaluation of explanations to the dependency‑parsing task by proposing a novel paradigm that exploits prepositional‑phrase attachment ambiguities, showing that sensitivity‑oriented methods preserve tree structures more faithfully than removal‑based approaches. Together, these contributions broaden the understanding of interpretation faithfulness, connect interpretability with model robustness, and provide new tools for assessing explanations across classification and structured prediction settings.

This positions AD‑GCL as the first GCL framework that couples contrastive training with learnable, graph‑specific augmentations and offers theoretical guarantees aligning the learned representations with the information‑bottleneck principle.

[ANSWER]: Generative adversarial nets (GANs) were introduced as a two‑player minimax game in which a generator transforms samples from a simple latent distribution into data space while a discriminator learns to distinguish generated samples from real ones.  The original formulation optimises a Jensen‑Shannon divergence, but many subsequent variants replace this divergence with alternative statistical distances—such as Wasserstein, least‑squares, f‑divergences, or integral probability metrics—to improve training stability, alleviate mode collapse and provide better gradient signals.  These modifications, while diverse in their theoretical motivations and empirical performance, share the common goal of learning an implicit model of a high‑dimensional data distribution without an explicit likelihood.

The task of co‑generation—producing a sample for a subset of the output space conditioned on the complementary part—has been explored in several application domains.  Early work on image‑to‑image translation learns a deterministic mapping between two fixed domains using encoder‑decoder or transformation networks; supervised variants require paired examples, whereas unsupervised approaches rely on cycle‑consistency or other regularisers to enforce bijective behaviour.  Although effective when the domain partition is known a priori, these methods do not generalise to arbitrary subsets specified at test time and therefore scale poorly when many possible partitions are of interest.

Optimization‑based techniques have been proposed to adapt GANs for conditional sampling when the conditioning region is unknown during training.  Methods that back‑propagate through the generator to infer a latent code matching the observed portion treat co‑generation as an inverse problem, iteratively updating the latent variable to minimise a reconstruction loss.  Similar ideas appear in approaches that directly maximise the conditional likelihood of missing data given observed data.  Empirically, these optimisation procedures often encounter a highly non‑convex, “ragged’’ energy landscape, which hampers convergence of gradient descent and can lead to failure in locating a suitable latent representation.

Conditional GANs (cGANs) extend the vanilla adversarial framework by conditioning both generator and discriminator on an auxiliary input (e.g., a label map, a sketch, or a semantic mask).  While cGANs excel at generating whole outputs from a given condition, they typically assume a fixed conditioning format and do not support arbitrary decomposition of the output space into multiple subsets without retraining separate models for each decomposition.

Multimodal Boltzmann machines and related energy‑based models learn a shared latent representation for heterogeneous modalities such as video–audio or image–text.  Encoder‑decoder architectures built on restricted Boltzmann machines can reconstruct one modality from another, and joint‑embedding methods map different data types into a common vector space where arithmetic operations produce new cross‑modal samples.  These approaches implicitly address co‑generation across modalities but rely on explicit probabilistic models and often require modality‑specific encoders, limiting their flexibility for arbitrary intra‑modal partitions.

Cross‑domain image generation techniques—including coupled GANs (CoGANs) and other weight‑sharing frameworks—train multiple generators (and sometimes discriminators) jointly so that they share a latent space while producing samples in distinct domains.  By iteratively updating a latent code to match observed partial data, these methods can perform tasks such as style transfer, attribute manipulation, or inpainting.  However, they typically optimise a loss that directly ties the latent code to a specific domain configuration and have reported issues with coverage and scalability when the number of possible sub‑domains grows.

A number of encoder‑decoder based style‑transfer, attribute‑transfer, and analogy‑learning methods map complete inputs to complete outputs, often leveraging perceptual or cycle‑consistency losses.  Although effective for whole‑image transformations, they require a dedicated decoder for each target subset, making them unsuitable for scenarios where the conditioning region is defined only at inference time.

Annealed importance sampling (AIS) is an algorithm originally devised to estimate partition‑function ratios by gradually transforming samples from a simple base distribution into samples from a target distribution through a sequence of intermediate distributions.  Beyond its original purpose, AIS can be employed as a generic sampler that produces high‑quality draws from complex, multimodal densities by leveraging the gradual annealing schedule.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) augments Markov‑chain Monte Carlo with auxiliary momentum variables and simulates Hamiltonian dynamics to propose distant, low‑autocorrelation moves in the state space.  By following trajectories that approximately conserve a Hamiltonian, HMC reduces the random‑walk behaviour typical of vanilla Metropolis‑Hastings updates, making it well‑suited for sampling from high‑dimensional, sharply curved probability landscapes.

Unlike conditional or encoder‑decoder approaches that require a predefined partition of the output space, our technique operates on any arbitrarily specified subset at test time without retraining. The lack of uncertainty awareness in existing unsupervised translation models limits their reliability when deployed on data that deviate from the training distribution.

Uncertainty estimation itself is commonly divided into epistemic and aleatoric components. Epistemic uncertainty reflects limited knowledge about model parameters and can be reduced with more data, whereas aleatoric uncertainty captures intrinsic noise in the observations. Bayesian deep‑learning techniques—including Monte‑Carlo dropout, deep ensembles, and variational inference—have been applied to a variety of vision tasks to estimate these uncertainties. In the context of image translation, such Bayesian approaches enable the extraction of predictive variance, which is valuable for downstream tasks and for informing clinicians about the trustworthiness of generated medical images.

Most existing probabilistic regression models assume per‑pixel heteroscedastic noise follows a Gaussian distribution. This assumption becomes problematic when outliers are present, as real‑world residuals often exhibit heavy‑tailed behavior that Gaussian models cannot capture. Recent work has highlighted the benefits of employing more flexible distributions, such as the generalized Gaussian, which subsumes Gaussian, Laplace, and heavier‑tailed families, allowing a better fit to diverse residual patterns and improving robustness to anomalous observations.

By modeling per‑pixel residuals with a generalized Gaussian distribution, the method captures heavy‑tailed error characteristics, thereby enhancing robustness to outliers and unseen perturbations. The probabilistic formulation yields explicit per‑pixel uncertainty estimates that correlate strongly with prediction errors. Extensive experiments on natural‑image benchmarks (including autonomous‑driving scenes, aerial maps, and facades) and on medical MRI data demonstrate competitive performance on standard test sets while delivering substantial gains in robustness under perturbed conditions, establishing the approach as a reliable alternative to existing deterministic and Bayesian translation models.

[ANSWER]: Task‑oriented dialogue systems have been studied extensively, with particular focus on the dialogue state tracking (DST) and natural language understanding (NLU) components that are essential for maintaining and interpreting the conversation context. Early work on DST primarily relied on encoding the dialogue context with convolutional, recurrent, or long‑short‑term memory networks and then independently predicting slot values. These approaches demonstrated strong performance on fixed‑domain benchmarks but lacked mechanisms for transferring knowledge to unseen schemas in new domains.  

To address the limitation of domain dependence, the schema‑guided dialogue paradigm was introduced. In this setting, natural‑language descriptions of intents, slots, and possible slot values are provided, enabling models to generalize across domains by leveraging the textual schema information. Several methods developed for the Schema‑Guided Dialogue (SGD) challenge exploit these descriptions to improve scalability, typically casting DST as a classification or extraction task that independently infers intent‑slot‑value pairs for the current turn.  

Sequence‑to‑sequence modeling has also been applied to DST. Models such as Sequicity adopt a two‑step approach, first encoding the dialogue history and generating a belief span, then producing a system response from that span. Hierarchical sequence‑to‑sequence architectures like COMER represent the relationships among intents, slots, and values through multi‑stage decoders. These works demonstrate the feasibility of treating DST as a generative translation problem, although they often employ hierarchical decoding structures and generate token sequences rather than pointer‑based representations.  

In parallel, the NLU task has traditionally been decomposed into separate intent classification and slot‑filling (sequence labeling) stages. Recent advances incorporate pretrained language models such as BERT to enhance feature representations, and some approaches jointly train classification and labeling components to capture interactions between intents and slots. These joint models improve accuracy but generally remain focused on single‑turn utterance processing rather than the multi‑turn, schema‑aware setting of DST.  

**In this work, we propose a unified approach that combines the strengths of schema‑guided DST and sequence‑to‑sequence generation. By employing BERT‑based encoders for both dialogue utterances and schema descriptions, the model obtains rich contextual embeddings for the conversation and the domain schema. An attention mechanism fuses these embeddings, enabling the decoder to generate pointers that directly reference intents, slots, and slot values. This flat, pointer‑based decoding eliminates the need for hierarchical structures while supporting categorical and non‑categorical slots, as well as unseen schemas. Because the same architecture can process a single user turn without schema context, it naturally extends to NLU, effectively unifying DST and NLU within a single framework. Empirical evaluation on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrates that this method achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance across both multi‑turn, schema‑guided scenarios and traditional single‑turn NLU tasks, confirming its simplicity, scalability, and effectiveness.

Empirical analyses have shown that these conventions limit the generality of SP policies and motivate the need for training regimes that produce coordination‑compatible behaviours.  

The zero‑shot coordination (ZSC) setting was proposed to address the incompatibility of SP policies by requiring agents to cooperate with previously unseen partners at test time.  Several families of algorithms have been developed for ZSC.  Other‑Play (OP) exploits known symmetries of the environment to constrain policy updates so that agents preserve these symmetries during training, yielding improved cross‑play and human‑AI performance in games such as Hanabi.  Ridge Rider (RR) leverages the relationship between environmental symmetries and repeated eigenvalues of the Hessian to encourage symmetry‑preserving policies without explicit symmetry information, though its computational cost has limited scalability to large‑scale RL problems.  Life‑Long Learning (LLL) approaches maintain a pool of pre‑trained agents and adapt new policies through continual interaction, often assuming access to symmetry information.  Off‑Belief Learning (OBL) trains agents with access to a simulator to infer and exploit belief structures, achieving strong ZSC results in Hanabi but requiring simulator‑level interactions during training.  

Parallel training techniques have been employed to improve robustness and sample efficiency in multi‑agent settings.  Population‑Based Training (PBT) was introduced for hyper‑parameter optimisation and later adapted to multi‑agent contexts, where a population of agents evolves jointly to avoid local optima and to produce less exploitable strategies in competitive or cooperative games.  PBT has also been applied to self‑play in Hanabi, demonstrating gains in policy quality. These approaches achieve notable OOD improvements on the VQA‑CP benchmark, which reverses answer distributions between training and test splits [4], although they often incur a drop in ID accuracy, highlighting the challenge of balancing both evaluations.

By assuming that answers are always present in the text, the task reduces to predicting start and end positions, a formulation that has driven many influential models [19]–[25]. However, directly predicting positions can introduce a positional bias, where models learn to associate answers with specific locations in the passage [26]. For example, training on data where answers consistently appear in the first sentence can cause a model to overly focus on that region. To assess robustness to such biases, a variant of the SQuAD dataset was introduced that deliberately skews answer position distributions, enabling evaluation of models’ resistance to positional shortcuts [26].

[ANSWER]: Metric learning seeks a distance function that brings semantically similar examples together while pushing dissimilar ones apart. In deep metric learning, an explicit non‑linear mapping from raw inputs to a low‑dimensional embedding space is learned, after which Euclidean distance exhibits the desired behavior. Although unsupervised formulations exist, the majority of work follows a supervised paradigm in which positive pairs share a class label and negative pairs belong to different classes. Loss functions for deep metric learning can be categorized as pair‑based or proxy‑based. Pair‑based losses operate on direct relationships between data points and have been defined over pairs, triplets, quadruplets, or higher‑order tuples. These losses capture fine‑grained data‑to‑data relations but are sensitive to label noise and outliers, and they often contain terms that become inactive once constraints are satisfied, yielding zero gradients. Consequently, hard‑example mining strategies such as semi‑hard or distance‑weighted sampling are commonly employed to provide informative training signals. Proxy‑based losses introduce learnable class proxies in the embedding space, replacing data‑to‑data interactions with data‑to‑proxy relations. By summarizing global class structure, proxy‑based approaches reduce computational overhead, generate more consistently non‑zero gradients, and typically require less aggressive mining, leading to faster convergence.

Input mixup linearly interpolates between two or more examples in the input space to augment data. Numerous extensions exploit the structure of specific domains, particularly images, by performing non‑linear interpolations or applying mixup to transformed representations. Manifold mixup extends the idea to intermediate feature representations, sometimes coupled with decoding back to the input space. In both input‑ and feature‑level mixup, target labels are interpolated linearly, and most studies have focused on cross‑entropy loss for classification tasks. The application of mixup to pairwise loss functions, such as those used in metric learning, has received considerably less attention.

Within deep metric learning, several works have explored interpolation strategies compatible with pairwise objectives. Embedding expansion and symmetrical synthesis interpolate pairs of embeddings deterministically within the same class, making them applicable to pair‑based losses. In contrastive representation learning, MoCHi interpolates anchor embeddings with negative samples without altering labels and employs a threshold to mitigate false negatives. The i‑mix approach interpolates anchor embeddings along with their virtual class labels in a linear fashion; it maintains a single positive per anchor while keeping all negatives clean, thereby limiting its ability to exploit interpolation for relative weighting of positives and negatives. These methods collectively illustrate a growing interest in leveraging interpolation for metric‑learning objectives, while highlighting challenges related to label handling and the balance between positive and negative contributions.

[ANSWER]: Transfer learning aims to improve performance on a target task by leveraging knowledge from source domains. Early approaches reused features extracted by a pretrained model, while later studies demonstrated that fine‑tuning the entire network yields higher transfer performance. Empirical investigations have examined fine‑tuning across diverse downstream scenarios, including image classification, few‑shot learning, medical imaging, and object detection. More recent work has identified limitations of vanilla fine‑tuning and proposed enhancements such as parameter or feature regularization, auxiliary tasks that capture category relationships or intrinsic structures, and analyses of layer‑wise transferability. These contributions largely focus on transferring knowledge from a single pretrained model.

One family estimates the transferability of each model and selects the most suitable one for a given target task, but accurate measurement of model transferability remains challenging and the approach discards the complementary knowledge present in other models. Another family aggregates information across models by concatenating features or merging parameters. However, these aggregation methods typically assume a model zoo in which all models share a common architecture or layer‑wise correspondence, an assumption that does not hold for heterogeneous collections of pretrained networks. This limitation motivates the study of more general settings where arbitrary pretrained models can be jointly leveraged without architectural constraints.

Conditional computation investigates mechanisms that activate only a subset of network components for each input example. Mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) architectures employ data‑dependent gating networks to select expert pathways, and sparsely‑gated MoE layers enable the training of extremely large models by activating a small number of experts per example. These works generally construct experts from homogeneous networks initialized randomly, rather than from a heterogeneous set of pretrained models that encode diverse knowledge.

We introduce a Hub‑Pathway framework that generates data‑dependent pathway weights to (i) select which pretrained models are activated for each input, (ii) aggregate the predictions of the activated models, and (iii) fine‑tune the selected models on the data that trigger them. To promote diverse exploration of pathway configurations we employ a noisy pathway generator together with an exploration loss, while the task‑specific loss drives exploitation of the most beneficial pathways. By operating without any assumptions on model architecture, dataset, or training paradigm, our approach overcomes the limitations of single‑model fine‑tuning, model‑level selection, and existing aggregation techniques, and extends conditional computation concepts to the setting of heterogeneous pretrained experts. Experiments on vision and reinforcement‑learning benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance for model‑hub transfer learning.

[ANSWER]: Robust control focuses on designing feedback controllers that guarantee performance in the presence of modeling uncertainties and external disturbances. Classical approaches formulate robustness criteria as linear matrix inequalities (LMIs), which can be solved efficiently with interior‑point or gradient‑based algorithms for problems of moderate size. These techniques often rely on linear or low‑order controllers to obtain provable stability, which can limit average‑case performance when richer nonlinear policies might be beneficial.  

Reinforcement learning (RL), and in particular deep RL, removes the restriction to simple controller structures by learning policies represented by neural networks through direct interaction with an environment. This paradigm has achieved notable success on a wide range of complex control tasks, as documented in several recent benchmarks and surveys. Because deep RL optimizes expected return without explicit safety constraints, most applications have been confined to simulated settings or highly controlled real‑world domains where failures are tolerable.  

To mitigate the safety and stability shortcomings of RL, a number of research directions have emerged. One line of work integrates control‑theoretic concepts, especially robust control, with the expressive power of neural‑network policies. Examples include methods that jointly learn Lyapunov functions and control policies to enforce stochastic stability, and approaches that cast continuous‑time control synthesis as min‑max differential games in which the controller and disturbance play opposing roles. These hybrid strategies aim to retain robustness guarantees while exploiting nonlinear policy representations.  

Another strand of research is safe RL, which seeks to enforce safety during learning and deployment. Many safe‑RL algorithms constrain exploration to regions of the state space that satisfy safety criteria, often assuming smooth dynamics that can be modeled with Gaussian processes or that satisfy Lipschitz continuity. Such assumptions enable probabilistic safety certificates but can be restrictive when dynamics exhibit sharp discontinuities.  

A third category leverages constrained Markov decision processes (C‑MDPs), where the objective is to maximize a discounted reward while keeping a separate discounted cost below a prescribed threshold. C‑MDPs do not require prior knowledge of the cost functions, yet they typically guarantee constraint satisfaction only at test time and may produce stochastic optimal policies whose constraints hold for only a subset of states.  

Parallel to these developments, differentiable optimization layers have become a popular tool for embedding optimization problems within neural networks. Recent work has introduced layers that solve quadratic programs, SAT instances, submodular optimization problems, cone programs, and other convex formulations in a way that permits gradient‑based learning. By embedding such layers, networks can be endowed with inductive biases that respect hard constraints of the underlying domain, enabling the projection of network outputs onto feasible sets defined by stability or safety requirements.

Early surveys [1, 2] established recall as the standard metric for comparing speed‑recall trade‑offs across different techniques.

A prominent family of ANN methods reduces the computational burden by operating in a lossy‑compressed domain.  These approaches follow a two‑stage pipeline: first they search a compact representation of the data (such as trees, graphs, or hash tables) to generate a candidate set, and then they compute exact distances between the query and the candidates to obtain the final top‑k results.  Because only a subset of points undergoes full distance evaluation, the overall cost is lowered while preserving high recall.

Various concrete instantiations of the compressed‑domain pipeline have been proposed.  Locality‑sensitive hashing (LSH) uses hash functions to map nearby points to the same buckets, performing a quick lookup followed by exact scoring [3, 4].  Tree‑based methods recursively partition the space and apply the two‑stage process at each node [5, 6].  Graph‑based techniques iteratively explore a proximity graph, alternating between candidate selection and distance computation until a stopping criterion is met [7].  Inverted file (IVF) systems first cluster the data with k‑means, then restrict search to the posting lists of the nearest centroids, again followed by exact rescoring [8–11].

Despite their success, compressed‑domain approaches face two fundamental challenges.  First, fractional search typically yields poor cache reuse because the candidate sets for different queries overlap only minimally, leading to suboptimal memory bandwidth utilization on modern hardware.  Second, tuning the speed‑recall balance is highly data‑dependent; the distance contrast between neighbors diminishes as dimensionality grows—a phenomenon documented in [12] as the “curse of high dimensionality.”  Moreover, theoretical work [13, 14] has shown that, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, sub‑linear‑time NN search with high recall is impossible for Euclidean, Manhattan, or Hamming distances, underscoring intrinsic limits of pruning‑based strategies.

The rise of specialized accelerators for machine‑learning workloads has opened new avenues for NN search.  Platforms such as Google’s TPU V3 and V4, and NVIDIA’s GPUs (V100, A100), provide orders of magnitude higher floating‑point throughput than conventional CPUs, especially for dense matrix‑multiplication kernels.  These devices expose dedicated compute units—tensor cores in NVIDIA GPUs [15] and systolic arrays in TPUs [16, 17]—that deliver markedly higher operation throughput for matrix‑oriented workloads compared with scalar or element‑wise instructions.  Accurately modeling the differing throughputs of these instruction classes is therefore essential for performance‑aware algorithm design.

Even with abundant FLOP/s, devising efficient selection primitives (e.g., top‑k or arg‑min) on accelerators remains an active research topic.  Recent studies [18–21] investigate parallel reduction, hierarchical heap, and warp‑level primitives to extract the smallest distances without incurring excessive synchronization or memory traffic.  As accelerator peak performance increases, the relative cost of selection can dominate the overall runtime, making it crucial to minimize selection overhead while preserving high recall.

The implementation is released as open‑source in JAX and TensorFlow, enabling reproducible research and practical deployment on modern accelerator hardware.

Moreover, the analyses are restricted to finite‑dimensional subspaces of the data domain and employ convergence criteria (weak convergence or Wasserstein distance) that do not guarantee convergence under the Kullback‑Leibler (KL) divergence, the loss actually optimized in maximum‑likelihood training. Indeed, an arbitrarily small distance in those metrics can correspond to an infinite KL divergence.

The relationship between conditioning of the coupling layers and the class of distributions that can be modeled has been examined in several studies. It has been shown that well‑conditioned affine couplings are sufficient to approximate log‑concave distributions that have been padded with additional dimensions, again with guarantees expressed in Wasserstein distance [9]. Deep extensions of functional maps learn descriptors from data rather than hand‑crafting them. Actor–critic formulations appear in various recent works, encompassing deep reinforcement learning, generative modeling, and sequence generation. In some registration pipelines, a value head predicts an appropriate granularity for shape mapping, influencing the temperature of a Gumbel‑Softmax distribution in the action head.

[ANSWER]: Score‑based and constraint‑based learning have long formed the two dominant paradigms for Bayesian network structure discovery.  Score‑based methods pair a decomposable scoring function such as BDeu with a heuristic search, e.g., Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) [2], to traverse the space of DAGs.  Constraint‑based approaches, exemplified by the PC and FCI algorithms [3, 4], rely on a series of conditional‑independence (CI) tests to infer the Markov equivalence class (CPDAG) that best fits the data.  While constraint‑based algorithms are attractive for their linear‑time scalability in the number of variables and their clear stopping criterion based on the maximal CI order, they are notoriously fragile: errors in high‑order CI tests, which are amplified in small‑sample regimes, can cascade into severely misspecified structures.  Hybrid techniques that interleave scoring and CI testing have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses [5], yet they still inherit the sensitivity of the underlying CI tests.  Our contribution directly addresses this vulnerability by embedding a non‑parametric bootstrap within a recursive constraint‑based framework: low‑order independencies, which are empirically stable, are reused throughout the recursion, while higher‑order tests are protected by increasing the number of bootstrap replicates.  Consequently, the resulting B‑RAI algorithm retains the computational efficiency of constraint‑based learning while dramatically improving robustness to sampling noise, a property not achieved by existing hybrid methods.

Recent work on exact MAP learning has focused on expanding the searchable space through clever encodings and branch‑and‑bound strategies, yielding algorithms that can guarantee optimality for domains up to roughly two dozen variables [6‑9].  Parallel efforts have produced methods that enumerate the top‑k most probable networks [10‑12] by exploiting specialized search spaces.  Although these advances represent important theoretical progress, their practical applicability remains limited to modest‑size problems because the underlying combinatorial explosion is only partially alleviated.  In contrast, B‑RAI is designed for high‑dimensional settings with hundreds of variables.  By organizing the search as a generative tree whose nodes correspond to scored CPDAGs for variable subsets, the algorithm decomposes the global problem into a hierarchy of smaller subproblems.  This recursive decomposition, together with bootstrap‑driven stabilization, enables B‑RAI to scale far beyond the variable limits of exact MAP solvers while still delivering high‑quality MAP estimates.

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques have become the standard for Bayesian model averaging in structure learning, sampling DAGs from the posterior distribution [13‑17].  Although MCMC provides a principled way to approximate posterior expectations, finite‑run guarantees are lacking: poor mixing, autocorrelation, and the prohibitive cost of evaluating large numbers of candidate graphs restrict their use to relatively small domains.  Our approach offers a deterministic alternative for model averaging: after constructing the B‑RAI tree, we introduce an efficient algorithm that draws exact samples of CPDAGs from the posterior encoded by the tree.  This sampling procedure leverages the hierarchical organization of the tree to produce independent draws without the convergence concerns inherent to MCMC, and it does so at a computational cost comparable to a single pass of the recursive learning phase.  Thus, the proposed framework unifies MAP estimation and posterior sampling within a single scalable pipeline, filling the gap between exact MAP methods and stochastic model‑averaging approaches.

An inducing‑point kernel is defined by a set of pseudo‑inputs and a base kernel, and its computational cost scales with the number of inducing points rather than the number of data points.  While such kernels are attractive for their simplicity, they live in a low‑dimensional reproducing‑kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) whose dimensionality is bounded by the number of inducing points, limiting model expressivity.  In contrast, our binary‑tree kernel builds an RKHS whose dimensionality grows exponentially with the depth of the tree, yet the kernel matrix can be assembled in \(O(n)\) space and inverted (approximately) in \(O(n)\) time.  Thus, we retain linear‑time and linear‑space complexity while providing a far richer functional class than traditional inducing‑point kernels.

Sparse Gaussian‑process regression (SGPR) selects a subset of training inputs and forms a low‑rank approximation of the kernel matrix, typically yielding a rank‑\(m\) matrix that can be inverted in \(O(m^{2}n)\) time.  The resulting predictive mean and covariance have compact closed‑form expressions, but the low rank of the approximation constrains the ability of the model to capture complex dependencies.  Our contribution is a kernel that is intrinsically low‑rank in a different sense: the kernel matrix can be expressed as a sum of sparse rank‑one components whose structure is dictated by the binary‑tree hierarchy.  This representation permits exact (up to a controllable approximation) inversion in linear time, offering the same scalability as SGPR while avoiding the severe expressivity bottleneck of a fixed low rank.

Sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGP) introduce a variational objective over inducing points and optimize both the inducing locations and kernel hyper‑parameters.  The variational formulation provides a principled bound on the marginal likelihood but still inherits the low‑dimensional RKHS of the underlying inducing‑point kernel.  Moreover, the variational bound complicates hyper‑parameter learning and can lead to biased posterior estimates when the inducing set is too small.  By contrast, the binary‑tree kernel is a bona‑fide kernel—not an approximation to another kernel—and its parameters are learned directly by maximizing the exact marginal likelihood (or its tractable approximation). Our binary‑tree kernel does not rely on spectral approximations; instead, it exploits a hierarchical partition of the input space, which yields a kernel that adapts to data structure without sacrificing the ability to model high‑dimensional interactions. [ANSWER]: Bayesian optimization applied directly to molecular discovery has traditionally relied on predefined libraries of candidate compounds. Early works demonstrated the feasibility of optimizing over fixed lists of molecules using acquisition functions such as expected improvement, but the approach is limited by the size of the library that can be enumerated in advance. Reported virtual libraries contain on the order of 10⁶–10⁸ molecules, which represents only a vanishing fraction of the astronomically large combinatorial space of all possible chemical structures. Consequently, these methods cannot explore novel regions of chemical space beyond the curated set.

A growing body of research has explored Bayesian optimization in latent spaces generated by deep autoencoders, enabling the search to span an effectively unbounded set of molecules. Within this line of work, two complementary strands have emerged. The first strand focuses on improving the training objectives of the autoencoder or the surrogate model so that the latent representation better captures the structure of the target property; examples include the incorporation of supervised or semi‑supervised losses, triplet constraints, and other regularizers that align latent distances with property differences. The second strand concentrates on enhancing the decoder component, often by imposing syntactic or semantic constraints such as grammar‑based decoding, graph‑based generation, or domain‑specific validity checks. These decoder improvements have been extended to other discrete design domains, including neural‑network architectures and kernel design for Gaussian processes, illustrating the broad applicability of latent‑space Bayesian optimization.

Several studies have investigated alternative search strategies for molecular design that do not rely on conventional Bayesian optimization. Evolutionary algorithms, including genetic algorithms, have been adapted to traverse chemical space by mutating and recombining molecular fragments. Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques have been employed to sample high‑probability regions of the space, while reinforcement‑learning approaches have trained policies to construct molecules atom by atom or to generate complete SMILES strings using autoregressive models. Although many of these methods can discover high‑performing compounds, they often require large numbers of function evaluations and therefore exhibit lower sample efficiency compared with Bayesian optimization‑based approaches.

In this work we introduce a method that directly addresses the limitations identified in the prior literature. First, we recognize that latent spaces produced by deep autoencoders remain high‑dimensional, which hampers the effectiveness of global acquisition functions such as expected improvement. To mitigate this issue we integrate a trust‑region‑based Bayesian optimization framework that operates locally within the latent space, thereby aligning the notion of locality in latent coordinates with locality in the original molecular domain. Second, we propose a semi‑supervised training scheme that jointly optimizes the variational autoencoder and a sparse Gaussian‑process surrogate, incorporating auxiliary objectives that encourage latent representations to respect the smoothness assumptions of the trust‑region model. Third, we design a transformer‑based encoder–decoder architecture built on a recent graph‑oriented molecular representation, which further improves the organization and validity of the latent space. Comprehensive experiments on six real‑world benchmark tasks demonstrate that the resulting algorithm achieves up to twenty‑fold improvements over state‑of‑the‑art latent‑space Bayesian optimization methods, while retaining the sample efficiency advantages of Bayesian optimization compared with evolutionary, MCMC, and reinforcement‑learning baselines.

[ANSWER]: Score‑based and constraint‑based learning have long formed the two dominant paradigms for Bayesian network structure discovery.  Score‑based methods pair a decomposable scoring function such as BDeu with a heuristic search, e.g., Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) [2], to traverse the space of DAGs.  Constraint‑based approaches, exemplified by the PC and FCI algorithms [3, 4], rely on a series of conditional‑independence (CI) tests to infer the Markov equivalence class (CPDAG) that best fits the data.  While constraint‑based algorithms are attractive for their linear‑time scalability in the number of variables and their clear stopping criterion based on the maximal CI order, they are notoriously fragile: errors in high‑order CI tests, which are amplified in small‑sample regimes, can cascade into severely misspecified structures.  Hybrid techniques that interleave scoring and CI testing have been proposed to mitigate these weaknesses [5], yet they still inherit the sensitivity of the underlying CI tests.  Our contribution directly addresses this vulnerability by embedding a non‑parametric bootstrap within a recursive constraint‑based framework: low‑order independencies, which are empirically stable, are reused throughout the recursion, while higher‑order tests are protected by increasing the number of bootstrap replicates.  Consequently, the resulting B‑RAI algorithm retains the computational efficiency of constraint‑based learning while dramatically improving robustness to sampling noise, a property not achieved by existing hybrid methods.

Recent work on exact MAP learning has focused on expanding the searchable space through clever encodings and branch‑and‑bound strategies, yielding algorithms that can guarantee optimality for domains up to roughly two dozen variables [6‑9].  Parallel efforts have produced methods that enumerate the top‑k most probable networks [10‑12] by exploiting specialized search spaces.  Although these advances represent important theoretical progress, their practical applicability remains limited to modest‑size problems because the underlying combinatorial explosion is only partially alleviated.  In contrast, B‑RAI is designed for high‑dimensional settings with hundreds of variables.  By organizing the search as a generative tree whose nodes correspond to scored CPDAGs for variable subsets, the algorithm decomposes the global problem into a hierarchy of smaller subproblems.  This recursive decomposition, together with bootstrap‑driven stabilization, enables B‑RAI to scale far beyond the variable limits of exact MAP solvers while still delivering high‑quality MAP estimates.

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques have become the standard for Bayesian model averaging in structure learning, sampling DAGs from the posterior distribution [13‑17].  Although MCMC provides a principled way to approximate posterior expectations, finite‑run guarantees are lacking: poor mixing, autocorrelation, and the prohibitive cost of evaluating large numbers of candidate graphs restrict their use to relatively small domains.  Our approach offers a deterministic alternative for model averaging: after constructing the B‑RAI tree, we introduce an efficient algorithm that draws exact samples of CPDAGs from the posterior encoded by the tree.  This sampling procedure leverages the hierarchical organization of the tree to produce independent draws without the convergence concerns inherent to MCMC, and it does so at a computational cost comparable to a single pass of the recursive learning phase.  Thus, the proposed framework unifies MAP estimation and posterior sampling within a single scalable pipeline, filling the gap between exact MAP methods and stochastic model‑averaging approaches.

The resurgence of interest in DPMs has been driven largely by their ability to produce high‑fidelity samples on image synthesis benchmarks [4, 5].

Early work on DPMs proposed a series of architectural and objective‑function refinements that substantially improved sample quality. In particular, the original discrete‑time diffusion model was shown to be equivalent to multi‑scale denoising score matching when diffusion variances are shared across dimensions, up to specific weightings per noise level [4]. Subsequent extensions introduced more expressive noise schedules and training tricks, leading to further gains in log‑likelihood performance [6].

A parallel line of research framed diffusion‑based generation as a multi‑scale denoising score‑matching problem and extended the methodology to continuous time. By interpreting the diffusion as a stochastic differential equation, these works derived sampling algorithms that reverse the forward diffusion process, enabling efficient generation without discretising the time axis [7, 8]. The continuous‑time perspective also opened the door to novel theoretical analyses of diffusion models.

Several recent studies derived variational lower bounds for continuous‑time diffusion models using stochastic differential equation formalisms. These works presented alternative derivations of the VLB, highlighted connections between the VAE‑style and score‑matching perspectives, and discussed conditions under which the two formulations coincide [9, 10, 11]. The analyses collectively deepened the understanding of how diffusion dynamics influence likelihood estimation.

Most prior diffusion models assumed a fixed forward diffusion schedule, parameterising the transition kernels at each timestep rather than the marginal statistics of the diffused data. Architectural innovations such as attention‑augmented U‑Nets, residual blocks, and conditioning mechanisms have been incorporated to improve expressivity, but the diffusion schedule itself has traditionally remained predetermined [4, 6, 8].

In this work we introduce a flexible family of diffusion‑based generative models that achieve new state‑of‑the‑art log‑likelihoods on standard image density‑estimation benchmarks (CIFAR‑10 and ImageNet). Leveraging this insight, we optimise the schedule to minimise the variance of the VLB estimator, accelerating training. The resulting models not only surpass autoregressive baselines on likelihood metrics but also enable near‑optimal lossless compression via a bits‑back scheme. By unifying and extending prior theoretical and architectural advances, our approach positions diffusion models as competitive likelihood‑based generators across both sample quality and density estimation.

[ANSWER]: Early information‑theoretic approaches to understanding deep neural networks focused on interpreting learning dynamics and memorization through mutual information between the training data and the learned parameters.  Foundational works established information‑stability bounds that relate generalization error to the mutual information between the algorithm’s output and the sample set.  These bounds, however, can become degenerate for continuous data distributions because the mutual information may be infinite or ill‑defined.  Subsequent studies highlighted this limitation and proposed alternative formulations that avoid such pathologies, paving the way for more robust information‑theoretic analyses of learning algorithms.

A second line of research introduced conditional mutual information (CMI) as a tool for deriving non‑degenerate generalization bounds.  By conditioning on a random subset of the training data, CMI‑based bounds circumvent the difficulties encountered by unconditional mutual information measures.  Extensions of this framework have been developed to bound the generalization error in terms of prediction outputs rather than internal model parameters, yielding some of the tightest information‑theoretic bounds available to date. By applying IntroD to the extractive QA setting, we use an ID‑teacher that captures the natural position distribution and an OOD‑teacher that imagines a uniform or counterfactual position distribution, enabling our student model to retain competitive SQuAD performance while substantially improving robustness to positional shifts.

Early work focused on models such as Hidden Markov Models, which employ discrete latent states, and Kalman Filters, which assume continuous states, providing foundational tools for capturing temporal dependencies in a variety of domains.

Deep auto‑regressive models, which factorize the joint likelihood of a sequence into a product of conditional distributions, have become a standard choice. These models typically use recurrent neural networks to encode past observations into hidden representations and then predict the next element with a parametric output distribution, often a unimodal or simple mixture density.  

Recognizing that deterministic hidden representations may limit expressive power, a line of work introduced stochastic latent variables into recurrent architectures. Early examples include the recurrent temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine and the RNN‑RBM, which embed latent variables within the recurrent dynamics. The development of variational auto‑encoding techniques enabled broader adoption of stochastic recurrent models, leading to variants such as temporal sigmoid belief networks, deep Kalman filters, deep Markov models, and Kalman variational auto‑encoders. These models combine nonlinear neural computations with latent‑variable flexibility and have been reported to achieve strong results on tasks such as raw audio generation.  

Despite successes in certain domains, the benefit of latent stochasticity does not uniformly translate across data modalities. In language modeling, some stochastic recurrent models have been observed to underperform deterministic baselines. Similarly, for image density estimation, fully deterministic auto‑regressive models like PixelCNN consistently surpass latent‑variable generative approaches. This mixed evidence has motivated investigations into the conditions under which stochastic latent variables provide practical advantages.  

Several studies have highlighted methodological factors that can affect comparative evaluations. Notably, the use of fully factorized output distributions restricts a model’s ability to capture intra‑step correlations, potentially biasing results in favor of stochastic models that can implicitly exploit such dependencies. Conversely, deterministic recurrent baselines constrained by the same factorization are prevented from modeling these correlations explicitly, leading to an uneven playing field.

By exposing the impact of evaluation bias and clarifying the role of intra‑step correlation modeling, our study provides a more balanced understanding of when stochastic latent variables are beneficial in sequential density estimation.

This paradigm has been widely adopted for automatic speech recognition, demonstrating gains when large quantities of unlabelled audio are available.

Multi‑task learning has been employed to mitigate data scarcity in speech‑to‑text tasks such as speech translation.  Prior studies combine supervised speech data with parallel text resources, training a single model on several related objectives (e.g., translation, transcription, language modelling). Another approach focuses on pre‑training the speech encoder using both speech and text inputs, but confines the learning to the encoder side, leaving the decoder to be trained separately. [ANSWER]: Previous research on continual learning (CL) has explored a variety of strategies to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Memory‑based approaches retain data from earlier tasks and incorporate it during the training of new tasks, either by replaying raw samples [1–3] or by explicitly reducing gradient interference [4,5]. Generative methods train models such as GANs [6,7] or autoencoders [8] to synthesize examples from past distributions, thereby improving memory efficiency. Other techniques store compact feature representations of previous instances and learn transformations that map past feature spaces onto the current one [9,10].

A complementary line of work constrains the flexibility of new tasks to preserve previously learned knowledge. Regularization‑based methods add penalties that discourage significant changes to important weights [11,12], while mask‑based approaches freeze subsets of the network [13,14]. Expanding network capacity by introducing additional parameters has also been proposed as a way to accommodate new tasks without overwriting old knowledge [15,16]. Some studies identify task‑specific pathways through the network, fixing the weights used for earlier tasks [17]. Others increase adaptability by employing specialized components such as hypernetworks [18], deep artificial neurons [19], or compositional structures [20].

Meta‑learning, the paradigm of learning to learn, has been applied to sequence learning [22,23] and to continual‑learning settings [24–27]. For example, combining instance prototypes from prior tasks with tailored loss functions can adapt model parameters to reduce forgetting [28]. Conditioning mechanisms that modify network weights have also been investigated: linear functions that squeeze activation maps to normalize convolutional outputs [29], and task‑dependent conditioning of convolutional layers using external cues such as questions in visual‑question‑answering systems [30].
