[ANSWER]: Metric learning aims to learn a distance metric that brings examples from the same class (positive pairs) close together while pushing examples from different classes (negative pairs) apart. In deep metric learning, an explicit non‑linear mapping from raw inputs to a low‑dimensional embedding space is learned so that Euclidean distances in this space exhibit the desired properties. Although unsupervised formulations exist, the majority of work follows a supervised paradigm in which positive and negative pairs are defined by matching or mismatching class labels. Loss functions for deep metric learning are commonly divided into pair‑based and proxy‑based families. Pair‑based losses operate directly on pairs, triplets, quadruplets or higher‑order tuples of examples, capturing fine‑grained data‑to‑data relationships but often suffering from sensitivity to noisy labels, outliers, and a prevalence of zero‑gradient terms that motivate hard‑example mining strategies such as semi‑hard or distance‑weighted sampling. Proxy‑based losses introduce learnable class representatives (proxies) that summarize each class in the embedding space, reducing computational cost and typically providing more consistent gradients, which can lessen the reliance on mining and accelerate convergence.

Input mixup linearly interpolates two or more samples in the input space and simultaneously interpolates their target labels, serving as a simple yet effective data‑augmentation technique. A large body of work extends this idea by exploiting domain‑specific structures to perform non‑linear interpolations for images, audio, and other modalities, and by applying mixup at intermediate layers of a network (manifold mixup) where the latent representations are mixed instead of raw inputs. Many of these approaches also employ a decoder to map mixed latent codes back to the input space. While the majority of mixup studies focus on classification tasks and cross‑entropy loss, the application of mixup to pairwise or metric‑learning losses remains relatively under‑explored.

Several recent works have investigated how to incorporate interpolation into pairwise loss functions. Embedding expansion and symmetrical synthesis interpolate pairs of embeddings within the same class in a deterministic manner, enabling the use of pair‑based losses but without modifying class labels. Proxy synthesis interpolates between class proxies, allowing label‑free mixing for proxy‑based losses, yet it can inadvertently generate false negatives when the interpolation factor approaches the extremes. In contrastive representation learning, MoCHi mixes an anchor with negative embeddings while avoiding label interpolation, and OptTransMix adopts a thresholding scheme to mitigate false negatives during interpolation. The i‑mix method linearly interpolates anchor embeddings together with their virtual class labels, but it only produces a single positive per anchor and retains clean negatives, limiting its ability to exploit relative weighting between positives and negatives. These approaches illustrate the challenges of defining and interpolating labels for pairwise objectives and highlight gaps in existing methodologies.

We propose a generic representation of binary “positive/negative” labels for anchor‑pair combinations and define a continuous interpolation scheme that preserves the semantic meaning of mixed pairs. [ANSWER]: Fair resource allocation via utility maximization has a long tradition in economics, mechanism design, and network management.  Classical works such as Palomar & Fischer (2006) and Eryilmaz & Srikant (2007) formulate fairness as the maximization of a concave utility function, but they assume a discrete‑time setting in which each action consumes a unit of time and the statistics of rewards are either known a priori or can be estimated offline.  Consequently, these models ignore the random, action‑dependent completion times that arise in many real‑world platforms (e.g., contractual hiring or cloud‑computing).  By contrast, our paper introduces a continuous‑time utility‑maximization framework that explicitly models stochastic completion times, incorporates deadline constraints, and operates without prior knowledge of reward or time distributions.  This positions our work as the first to unify fairness criteria (proportional, max‑min, reward‑maximizing) with time‑efficient decision making in a setting where both rewards and durations must be learned online.

The only existing continuous‑time treatment of fair allocation is Neely (2012), which develops an offline stochastic‑control solution under the assumption that first‑order statistics of the underlying processes are known.  While Neely’s approach provides valuable insights into the structure of optimal policies, it does not address the algorithmic challenges of learning these statistics or of delivering finite‑time performance guarantees.  Building on Neely’s formulation, we derive a tractable approximation to the optimal offline policy using Lagrange duality and renewal theory, and we prove that this approximation is asymptotically optimal.  Moreover, we extend the offline results to the online setting by designing a dual‑ascent algorithm that achieves a $\tilde O(B^{-1/2})$ regret bound, thereby advancing the state of the art from purely offline analysis to provably efficient online learning.

Lyapunov‑drift and drift‑plus‑penalty methods have become standard tools for dynamic optimization in queueing and wireless networks (e.g., Neely 2006, Eryilmaz & Srikant 2009).  Existing applications typically assume that random quantities (such as channel states or service times) are observed before the control decision, or that their first‑ and second‑order moments are known.  These “opportunistic” assumptions are violated in our target applications, where the controller must decide on a worker and a deadline before the actual completion time is realized, and where the statistical model must be learned.  Our work is the first to integrate Lyapunov‑drift analysis with online learning of unknown completion‑time and reward distributions, while simultaneously enforcing fairness through a general utility function and improving time‑efficiency via controlled deadlines.

The bandits‑with‑knapsacks (BwK) literature addresses online learning under resource constraints, focusing on maximizing expected total reward while consuming a stochastic budget (Badanidiyuru & Kleinberg 2018; Tran‑Thanh et al. 2012).  Extensions that incorporate continuous‑time dynamics (Cayci et al. 2019) or concave rewards with convex constraints (Agrawal & De Rotto 2014) still prioritize reward maximization and either ignore fairness considerations or lack explicit deadline mechanisms.  In contrast, our framework augments the BwK setting with a fairness‑oriented utility function, action‑dependent random completion times, and hard deadlines that guarantee time‑efficient budget usage.  The resulting algorithm retains low computational complexity while delivering regret guarantees that are comparable to, and in some regimes superior to, those of existing BwK approaches.

Finally, recent works on online convex optimization with constraints (e.g., Zhou & Jiang 2020) achieve vanishing constraint violation by solving linear programs at each round, but they do not enforce strict time budgets, nor do they model the interplay between random service durations and fairness.  By contrast, our contribution lies in a unified treatment of (i) continuous‑time stochastic dynamics, (ii) fairness‑driven utility maximization, (iii) deadline‑based time‑efficiency, and (iv) online learning with provable $\tilde O(B^{-1/2})$ regret.  This combination of features fills a gap in the literature and provides a versatile methodological foundation for a broad class of fairness‑sensitive sequential decision problems.

In contrast, RoMe is trained in a self‑supervised manner on automatically generated perturbations, which eliminates the need for costly human labels while preserving strong correlation with human assessments across diverse NLG tasks. Early paired approaches such as conditional adversarial networks [1,2,3] directly minimize pixelwise losses, while unpaired methods introduced adversarial training together with cycle‑consistency or distribution‑matching constraints to infer a joint distribution from marginal samples [4,5,6,7,8]. Although these techniques succeed in producing visually plausible results, they all learn a single fixed mapping from source to target, which precludes the ability to express predictive uncertainty and makes the models vulnerable to outliers and distribution shifts at test time. In contrast, our Uncertainty‑aware Generalized Adaptive Cycle Consistency (UGAC) framework retains the adversarial and cycle‑consistency objectives of the unpaired literature but augments them with a probabilistic residual model that captures heavy‑tailed error distributions. By doing so, UGAC not only preserves the high‑quality translations of deterministic baselines but also endows each output pixel with a calibrated uncertainty estimate, addressing a key limitation of existing deterministic translators.

Uncertainty estimation for deep generative models has been explored mainly through Bayesian deep learning and heteroscedastic regression, where per‑pixel variance is often assumed Gaussian [9,10,11,12]. While these approaches provide a measure of aleatoric noise, the Gaussian assumption is fragile in the presence of outliers, which commonly follow heavier‑tailed distributions in real‑world imaging scenarios. Recent works have begun to consider more expressive noise models, yet they remain limited to supervised or paired settings and do not integrate uncertainty into the cycle‑consistency framework. UGAC advances this line of research by modeling per‑pixel residuals with a generalized Gaussian distribution, a family that subsumes Gaussian, Laplace, and heavier‑tailed laws. This choice enables robust learning under noisy or corrupted inputs and yields uncertainty scores that correlate strongly with prediction errors, a property not demonstrated by prior Bayesian or heteroscedastic translation methods.

The need for reliable uncertainty quantification is especially acute in safety‑critical domains such as medical image translation, where missing modalities or acquisition artifacts can jeopardize clinical decisions. [ANSWER]: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) originated with behavior cloning, which pre‑trains a policy by minimizing prediction error on state‑action pairs collected from an expert. Although simple, behavior cloning suffers from distribution shift and error accumulation as the learned policy deviates from the demonstrated trajectories. To mitigate these issues, DAgger introduced a no‑regret framework that iteratively queries an oracle for corrective actions, at the cost of requiring online access to the expert. More recent LfD methods have embraced inverse reinforcement learning, which seeks a reward function that renders the expert behavior optimal; the recovered reward can then be optimized with standard reinforcement‑learning algorithms. A prominent instance of this paradigm is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), which casts imitation as a distribution‑matching problem and employs a generative‑adversarial network to minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the expert and learner state‑action distributions. Building on GAIL, numerous works have explored alternative reinforcement‑learning back‑ends or substituted different statistical divergences to improve imitation performance, yet the majority of these approaches remain on‑policy, requiring fresh environment interactions at each policy update and consequently incurring high sample costs.

To address the sample inefficiency of on‑policy imitation, several off‑policy extensions have been proposed. DAC adapts the GAIL objective to reuse past experiences stored in a replay buffer, thereby reducing the need for on‑policy data collection. Similar replay‑based strategies appear in other works that recycle cached transitions for policy improvement. A common limitation of these methods is that they often ignore the distributional discrepancy introduced when substituting the true on‑policy occupancy with an off‑policy approximation, which can lead to a drift from the intended objective. ValueDICE offers another off‑policy route by reformulating the on‑policy imitation loss using the DICE framework; however, it relies on access to expert actions, rendering it unsuitable for settings where only observations are available. Consequently, off‑policy imitation methods that do not require expert actions remain an open challenge.

Learning from Observations (LfO) tackles the more restrictive scenario in which expert action labels are absent. Model‑free LfO approaches typically extend the adversarial imitation paradigm to state‑only data. GAIfO applies the GAIL framework with a discriminator that receives only states, enabling imitation without action information. IDDM analyzes the theoretical gap between LfD and LfO objectives and shows that maximizing the mutual information between latent actions and observed states can partially bridge this gap, achieving performance comparable to GAIL while still relying on on‑policy data. Other model‑free methods assume a ranking over observation trajectories and construct reward functions accordingly; these techniques also inherit the sample‑inefficiency of on‑policy learning.

Model‑based LfO methods introduce dynamics models to compensate for the missing action signals. Forward‑model approaches learn a transition model and use it to synthesize pseudo‑actions or to plan directly; while effective for finite‑horizon tasks, they may struggle with long‑horizon or infinite‑horizon problems due to the need for time‑dependent policies. Inverse‑model approaches infer the missing actions by training a mapping from consecutive observations to the underlying action, after which standard behavior‑cloning can be applied. This strategy, exemplified by Behavior Cloning from Observations (BCO), inherits the limitations of behavior cloning and additionally requires strong assumptions such as deterministic, injective dynamics to guarantee accurate action recovery. Other recent works consider mismatched dynamics or viewpoints between expert and learner observations, further expanding the scope of LfO research.

In contrast to prior methods, the present work introduces a sample‑efficient LfO algorithm that operates fully off‑policy without requiring expert actions. By deriving an upper bound on the LfO objective, the approach enables principled off‑policy optimization while explicitly accounting for the distribution shift between on‑policy and replay‑buffer samples. To further accelerate learning, the method incorporates a regularization term that promotes mode‑covering distribution matching; under deterministic dynamics this regularizer is implemented via an inverse action model learned from the replay buffer. The resulting algorithm achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on challenging locomotion benchmarks, matching or surpassing existing methods in both asymptotic return and sample complexity, thereby addressing the limitations of on‑policy dependence, action‑free requirements, and theoretical guarantees highlighted in earlier work.

When the quality functions themselves are differentially private mechanisms, a distinct selection problem arises. The optimality of the exponential mechanism has also been examined. However, standard deep‑RL algorithms offer no explicit safety or robustness guarantees, which has confined their deployment to simulated or otherwise low‑risk settings.  A growing body of work attempts to combine RL with control‑theoretic ideas—such as jointly learning Lyapunov functions, solving min‑max differential games, or incorporating robust‑control specifications into the learning objective. Although simple, behavior cloning suffers from distribution shift and error accumulation as the learned policy deviates from the demonstrated trajectories. To mitigate these issues, DAgger introduced a no‑regret framework that iteratively queries an oracle for corrective actions, at the cost of requiring online access to the expert. More recent LfD methods have embraced inverse reinforcement learning, which seeks a reward function that renders the expert behavior optimal; the recovered reward can then be optimized with standard reinforcement‑learning algorithms. A prominent instance of this paradigm is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL), which casts imitation as a distribution‑matching problem and employs a generative‑adversarial network to minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the expert and learner state‑action distributions. Building on GAIL, numerous works have explored alternative reinforcement‑learning back‑ends or substituted different statistical divergences to improve imitation performance, yet the majority of these approaches remain on‑policy, requiring fresh environment interactions at each policy update and consequently incurring high sample costs.

To address the sample inefficiency of on‑policy imitation, several off‑policy extensions have been proposed. DAC adapts the GAIL objective to reuse past experiences stored in a replay buffer, thereby reducing the need for on‑policy data collection. Similar replay‑based strategies appear in other works that recycle cached transitions for policy improvement. A common limitation of these methods is that they often ignore the distributional discrepancy introduced when substituting the true on‑policy occupancy with an off‑policy approximation, which can lead to a drift from the intended objective. ValueDICE offers another off‑policy route by reformulating the on‑policy imitation loss using the DICE framework; however, it relies on access to expert actions, rendering it unsuitable for settings where only observations are available. Consequently, off‑policy imitation methods that do not require expert actions remain an open challenge.

Learning from Observations (LfO) tackles the more restrictive scenario in which expert action labels are absent. Model‑free LfO approaches typically extend the adversarial imitation paradigm to state‑only data. GAIfO applies the GAIL framework with a discriminator that receives only states, enabling imitation without action information. IDDM analyzes the theoretical gap between LfD and LfO objectives and shows that maximizing the mutual information between latent actions and observed states can partially bridge this gap, achieving performance comparable to GAIL while still relying on on‑policy data. Other model‑free methods assume a ranking over observation trajectories and construct reward functions accordingly; these techniques also inherit the sample‑inefficiency of on‑policy learning.

Model‑based LfO methods introduce dynamics models to compensate for the missing action signals. Forward‑model approaches learn a transition model and use it to synthesize pseudo‑actions or to plan directly; while effective for finite‑horizon tasks, they may struggle with long‑horizon or infinite‑horizon problems due to the need for time‑dependent policies. Inverse‑model approaches infer the missing actions by training a mapping from consecutive observations to the underlying action, after which standard behavior‑cloning can be applied. This strategy, exemplified by Behavior Cloning from Observations (BCO), inherits the limitations of behavior cloning and additionally requires strong assumptions such as deterministic, injective dynamics to guarantee accurate action recovery. Classical embedded techniques include the LASSO, which imposes an ℓ₁ penalty to encourage sparse coefficient vectors, and its extensions to non‑linear models and deep networks. These methods focus on selecting individual features and do not explicitly model interactions among them.

A parallel line of work addresses situations where variables are naturally organized into groups. The Group LASSO replaces the ℓ₁ penalty with an ℓ₂ norm on each predefined group, enabling entire groups to be retained or discarded together. Similar extensions have been proposed for other regularizers, including Group‑SLOPE, SCAD‑L₂, and hierarchical LASSO, which incorporate structured penalties that respect a known grouping hierarchy. Bayesian formulations have also been adapted to the group setting by placing sparsity‑inducing priors on group‑level parameters. In the model‑free domain, the Knockoff framework generates synthetic covariates that preserve the joint distribution of the original features; its group‑wise variants construct knockoffs for entire groups, allowing false‑discovery‑rate control when groups are selected based on a suitable statistic.

Across these group‑selection approaches, a common assumption is the availability of a predefined partition or collection of candidate groups. The methods can only choose among the supplied candidates and cannot infer new groupings from the data. Consequently, they are unsuitable when the appropriate grouping structure is unknown, when groups may overlap, or when interactions do not align with any externally imposed partition.

In contrast, the present work tackles the problem of uncovering predictive groups of features without any prior grouping information. It formalises composite feature selection as an extension of standard selection, defining groups in terms of both linear and non‑linear interactions among variables. To identify such groups, a novel deep‑learning architecture is introduced that ensembles multiple feature‑selection models, enforcing sparsity, minimal overlap, and joint predictivity across the discovered groups. A new similarity metric based on the Jaccard index is proposed to evaluate how closely the recovered groups match ground‑truth structures. Domain generalization seeks to learn models that perform well on unseen target domains without any target data at training time. The problem was first introduced in [10] and formally defined in [11]. Early work focused on learning domain‑invariant representations by minimizing feature dissimilarities across source domains [11], [12]. This line of research has been extended by numerous methods that impose invariance constraints on learned features [13]–[17]. Meta‑learning has also been applied to domain generalization. Several approaches treat domain generalization as a meta‑learning problem, training on a set of source domains and evaluating adaptation on held‑out domains [23]–[26]. Model‑agnostic meta‑learning (MAML) was introduced for this purpose in [27] and later enhanced with global and local regularization techniques [29]. Common experimental protocols partition source domains into meta‑source and meta‑target subsets to mimic the adaptation process during training [24], [25].

Test‑time adaptation methods aim to adjust a pretrained source model to unseen target data at inference time. Some approaches combine supervised and self‑supervised objectives during source training and then fine‑tune the model on target data using only the self‑supervised loss [31]. Others remove the self‑supervised component and rely on entropy minimization for test‑time fine‑tuning [32]. A different strategy learns a domain‑embedding network from unsupervised source data; the embedding is then estimated for a target domain using many unlabeled target samples, enabling adaptation without explicit fine‑tuning [33]. These techniques typically require additional steps such as fine‑tuning or processing batches of target samples. Test‑time augmentation has also been employed to improve robustness during inference [34], providing another avenue for adapting models to test‑time variations.

The concept of Sufficient Input Subsets (SIS) has been introduced to probe whether a model can arrive at a confident decision based on a minimal set of input pixels. Studies have shown that SIS can expose over‑interpretation, where classifiers succeed with sparse, non‑human‑interpretable pixel patterns. To evaluate robustness beyond standard accuracy, a variety of test sets have been proposed that explicitly target distribution shifts: ImageNet‑v2 offers a re‑sampled test distribution; ImageNet‑A contains natural adversarial examples; ImageNet‑R and ImageNet‑Sketch present artistic renditions and sketches; ObjectNet controls object placement and viewpoint; and SI‑Score provides synthetic variations in object location, rotation, and scale. Explainability techniques aim to reveal the regions that drive a model’s predictions. Gradient‑based methods constitute a widely used family, often refined by incorporating input signals to produce sharper relevance maps. Alternative approaches include attribution propagation grounded in axiomatic principles and permutation‑based methods that approximate Shapley values. For transformer‑based vision models, combining gradient information with attention weights has been shown to yield more faithful visual explanations. Such methods have uncovered tendencies of models to neglect foreground objects or to over‑emphasize background areas in their relevance visualizations.

[ANSWER]: Bayesian posterior sampling under differential privacy has traditionally relied on the “one‑posterior‑sample” (OPS) mechanism, which observes that drawing a single sample from a posterior whose log‑likelihood is Lipschitz or bounded yields a DP guarantee (e.g., [1]–[4]). Subsequent work extended this idea to tempered posteriors and to Rényi‑DP ([5]), but all of these approaches assume access to an exact sample from the target distribution. In practice exact sampling is rarely attainable, and the privacy guarantee therefore becomes conditional on an unverifiable assumption. By contrast, our algorithm does not depend on exact sampling; the privacy analysis is based on a decomposition of the Barker acceptance test that yields a strict, non‑asymptotic Rényi‑DP bound regardless of the chain’s convergence state. This eliminates the conditionality that limits OPS‑based methods and enables privacy‑preserving inference for arbitrary models, including those with discrete parameters.

A second line of DP Bayesian work perturbs sufficient statistics of exponential‑family models using the Laplace mechanism. Early proposals ([6] and successors [3], [7]–[10]) exploit the fact that sufficient statistics are low‑dimensional, allowing efficient noise injection and unconditional privacy guarantees. However, these methods are confined to exponential‑family structures and often ignore the injected noise during downstream inference, leading to biased posterior estimates. Later refinements such as [10] incorporate the noise distribution into the posterior, improving variance estimates but still remaining model‑specific. Our contribution departs from this paradigm by providing a generic MCMC framework that works for any probabilistic model, without requiring the existence of sufficient statistics or model‑specific adjustments, while still delivering rigorous DP guarantees.

Gradient‑based DP MCMC algorithms, including differentially private Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and stochastic‑gradient Langevin dynamics, introduce noise to gradient evaluations and obtain privacy through advanced composition tools such as the moments accountant ([2], refined in [11]). These methods offer unconditional privacy for differentiable, Lipschitz log‑likelihoods, but their reliance on gradients restricts them to continuous‑parameter models and precludes application to discrete or non‑differentiable settings. Moreover, the privacy loss accumulates with the number of iterations. Our approach sidesteps gradient computation entirely by operating on the acceptance test itself; consequently it applies equally well to models with discrete variables and yields a privacy bound that is independent of the number of MCMC steps, addressing a key limitation of gradient‑based DP MCMC.

Finally, subsampling‑based MCMC techniques aim to reduce computational cost by evaluating the acceptance test on mini‑batches of data, a strategy explored in the literature on non‑private MCMC ([13]–[16]) and more recently adapted to DP settings ([14]). Existing subsampled DP methods often require adaptive batch sizes that can grow to the full dataset, undermining the privacy amplification benefits of subsampling. Our work builds on the Barker acceptance test formulation to design a principled subsampling approximation whose privacy loss can be tightly quantified using Rényi‑DP. We further improve upon the subsampling correction of [13] by deriving a more accurate noise distribution, thereby achieving stronger privacy guarantees and higher statistical efficiency while maintaining fixed, small batch sizes that fully exploit privacy amplification.

Curriculum‑based strategies have also been explored, aligning target samples with dynamically selected source examples to exploit varying transferability across the source data.

Despite the success of these techniques, aligning distributions in parallel with the classification objective can sometimes diminish discriminative information. To mitigate this issue, a restoration module has been added to recover task‑relevant details that may be lost during alignment. Meta‑learning strategies have been proposed to coordinate the optimization of alignment and classification objectives, reducing potential contradictions between them. Additionally, feature decoupling methods separate domain‑invariant from domain‑specific components, aligning only the invariant part for tasks such as unsupervised person re‑identification. These lines of work collectively illustrate the evolution of UDA methods toward more nuanced and task‑aware alignment mechanisms.

[ANSWER]: Recovering private training data from shared gradients has become a central research theme in federated learning. Early work such as Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG) introduced a gradient‑based inversion technique that can reconstruct individual training samples without auxiliary generative models or prior information. Although DLG demonstrated the feasibility of gradient inversion, its performance deteriorates sharply when the model architecture deviates from simple fully‑connected networks or when weight initialization is varied. By contrast, our proposed CAFE is designed to operate robustly across diverse VFL architectures and to remain effective under realistic initialization schemes, thereby overcoming the generalizability limitations of DLG.

Analytical approaches that extract information directly from gradients have also been explored. One line of work focuses on label recovery by exploiting the linear relationship between gradients and class logits, while another derives input features before the first fully‑connected (FC) layer through closed‑form solutions. These methods, however, are constrained to single‑sample settings and cannot be scaled to the batch regime that is typical in practical VFL training. CAFE extends the analytical insight to the batch scenario by jointly recovering the loss gradients with respect to the intermediate representations, enabling reliable reconstruction of many samples simultaneously.

A subsequent family of techniques formulates the inversion problem as a system of linear equations, attempting to solve for batch inputs before the FC layer. Such methods rely on strong assumptions—e.g., full rank of the activation matrix or independence among samples—that rarely hold in real‑world VFL deployments. Consequently, they lack guaranteed recovery when these assumptions are violated. In contrast, CAFE incorporates a theoretical analysis that quantifies the conditions under which batch recovery succeeds, and it relaxes the restrictive assumptions by leveraging the inherent alignment of data indices across parties in vertical FL.

Some researchers have argued that convolutional layers can be reshaped into equivalent FC layers, suggesting that gradient inversion could be applied uniformly across network types. Nevertheless, the gradients of the original convolutional operation differ from those of the reshaped FC representation, which hampers accurate inversion. CAFE explicitly addresses this mismatch by modelling the true convolutional gradient flow and integrating it into the recovery pipeline, thereby preserving fidelity when reconstructing data processed by convolutional components.

Building on DLG, later works introduced custom loss functions or regularizers—such as Gaussian‑kernel‑based gradient differences or recursive attack procedures—to improve stability across architectures. While these refinements enhance reconstruction quality for small batches, they still experience significant degradation as batch size grows. Our method departs from heuristic loss engineering by providing a principled three‑step recovery process (gradient of loss w.r.t. first FC output, input reconstruction to the FC layer, and final data recovery) that scales gracefully to large batches without sacrificing accuracy.

The most recent gradient inversion algorithms, exemplified by GradInversion, achieve batch reconstruction by iteratively optimizing noise vectors against gradient constraints. Their theoretical foundations, however, depend on strong assumptions about data distribution and gradient linearity, and empirical evaluations have been limited to modest batch sizes (≤ 48). CAFE not only surpasses these batch limits—demonstrating successful recovery on substantially larger batches in vertical FL—but also supplies explicit recovery guarantees that clarify when and why the attack succeeds.

Overall, the existing literature either targets horizontal FL, assumes single‑sample inputs, or imposes impractical conditions that restrict batch scalability. By integrating vertical federated learning specifics, offering rigorous theoretical guarantees, and proposing a practical defense based on fake gradients, CAFE positions itself as the first comprehensive solution that both reveals the severity of large‑batch data leakage in VFL and provides actionable mitigation strategies.

An alternative and increasingly dominant line of work employs domain‑adversarial learning, in which a domain discriminator is trained to distinguish source from target features while the feature extractor is encouraged to produce representations that confuse the discriminator. This adversarial formulation has become the backbone of most recent high‑performing UDA approaches.

Building on the seminal domain‑adversarial neural network (DANN), a large family of variants has been proposed to strengthen the alignment signal. Conditional adversarial networks condition the discriminator on class predictions, thereby injecting label‑related information into the alignment process. Multi‑discriminator designs allocate a separate domain classifier per class to achieve class‑wise alignment. Other extensions perform simultaneous alignment at multiple granularities (e.g., class, group, and domain) and enforce gradient consistency across these levels. Heuristic‑driven methods introduce domain‑specific representations or curriculum‑based sample selection to guide the alignment toward more transferable source instances. Collectively, these techniques refine the adversarial objective but retain the fundamental paradigm of aligning whole feature vectors across domains.

Despite the progress, most adversarial UDA methods treat domain alignment as an auxiliary task that runs in parallel with the primary classification objective. This separation can cause the alignment process to interfere with discriminative information, leading to a loss of class‑specific features. ANSWER: Previous studies on TDMR (Task-Dataset-Metric-Result) extraction primarily rely on data sources such as NLP-progress or PapersWithCode. While these sources are popular, they lack rigorous quality control, including standardized TDM entity representation and complete publication coverage. Some efforts, such as [1] and [2], go further by extracting TDM triples and result values, and normalizing them for leaderboard construction. However, these approaches are constrained by their reliance on a closed domain, requiring extracted triples to match a pre-defined TDM taxonomy. Other studies, such as [3] and [4], only extract TDM triples without result values, thereby forgoing leaderboard construction. Meanwhile, [6] focuses on extracting result values, but only in the context of pre-defined TDM triples, making it similar in limitation to [1]. Consequently, these methods are not adaptable to the dynamic nature of emerging benchmarks, where new tasks, datasets, and metrics are frequently introduced.
In a parallel research thread, scientific leaderboards have been treated as a form of scientific knowledge graphs composed of Task, Dataset, and Metric entities. Information extraction in this context has been widely studied, as seen in works such as [5, 7, 8, 9, 10]. These studies typically focus on linking scientific content to structured entities but often assume that the schema or triples are known in advance.
In contrast to prior work, our approach addresses several critical limitations. We construct our dataset manually from publications to ensure comprehensive TDMR annotations, rather than relying on incomplete or unstandardized third-party sources. We normalize TDMR tuples for accurate leaderboard construction and propose novel experimental settings that reflect realistic, dynamic scenarios, including cold-start conditions without any pre-defined TDM taxonomy. By simultaneously constructing a scientific knowledge graph and linking publications to it in an open-domain setting, our method is inherently adaptable to the evolving research landscape.

[ANSWER]: Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) builds on the success of macro‑operators and abstraction in classical planning, inspiring a substantial body of work that decomposes control across multiple levels of abstraction.  Early approaches emphasized the intuitive benefits of such decompositions—simpler sub‑problems and the ability to make long‑term decisions—but more recent analyses have highlighted that, for modern neural‑network‑based agents, the principal advantage of HRL often lies in its enhanced exploration capabilities.  By separating the acquisition of low‑level policies (options or skills) from high‑level decision making, HRL can dramatically accelerate learning on downstream tasks.

A diverse set of methods has been proposed for discovering low‑level primitives.  Some techniques rely on random walk data to identify useful behaviours, while others formulate mutual‑information objectives that encourage diversity among options.  Additional strands of research exploit datasets of agent or expert trajectories, motion‑capture recordings, or dedicated pre‑training tasks to shape the skill space.  These approaches differ in the source of supervision and the assumptions they make about the environment, yet they share the goal of producing reusable behaviours that can be composed by higher‑level policies.

The usefulness of learned skills across many downstream tasks is constrained by a trade‑off between generality and specificity.  Many prior works resolve this trade‑off in favour of specificity, often by selecting benchmark domains that align closely with the induced prior.  Classic navigation problems in grid‑world mazes and simulated robotic locomotion tasks dominate the evaluation landscape, where translating the robot’s centre of mass is the primary required skill.  In such settings, skills are frequently defined by partitioning the state space according to the agent’s position or by leveraging position‑heavy reward signals, thereby embedding an explicit locomotion prior.  Other studies that address non‑navigation environments introduce tailored pre‑training objectives or rely on in‑domain motion‑capture data to bias skill acquisition toward particular behaviours.

In contrast, recent efforts have begun to explore skill discovery without external supervision or task‑specific pre‑training designs, aiming to learn low‑level behaviours that do not encode a fixed bias toward any single type of motion.  These works seek to retain flexibility in the skill set, allowing downstream tasks to select the most appropriate behaviours dynamically rather than being constrained by a predetermined prior.  

Building on these lines of research, the present work proposes an unsupervised pre‑training framework that generates a hierarchy of skills with increasing complexity, each controlling a variable subset of the robot’s configuration.  A three‑level hierarchical policy is introduced to automatically select among these skills, determine target configurations, and execute the corresponding low‑level actions, thereby enabling dynamic trade‑offs between generality and specificity during downstream learning.  To evaluate the approach, a benchmark suite of sparse‑reward tasks for bipedal robots is released, extending assessment beyond traditional navigation problems and facilitating systematic comparison of motor‑skill and HRL methods.  Extensive experiments demonstrate how prior knowledge embedded in skills affects exploration efficiency, and show that the proposed hierarchical skill framework achieves superior performance relative to existing unsupervised skill discovery and hierarchical RL baselines.

Both strands have produced extensive literature that explores the internal workings of neural language models.

A widely adopted methodology is the probing framework, in which auxiliary classifiers are trained on frozen representations to predict linguistic properties such as morphology, syntax, or semantics. Probing has been applied to a broad range of granularity levels—from character‑ and word‑level tasks to sub‑sentence phenomena—providing quantitative evidence of the information retained at different network depths. Investigations that go beyond probing to discover latent concepts directly in the representation space have also emerged. These studies demonstrate that models can encode both linguistically motivated and novel, task‑specific concepts, although they often rely on supervised signals to define the concepts of interest.

Critiques of the probing paradigm have highlighted methodological concerns such as the dependence on probe complexity, the influence of random seeds, and the risk of conflating representational capacity with learnability. One line of work uses the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, while a follow‑up employs the trace of the Hessian to gauge each layer’s susceptibility to perturbations. The underlying intuition is that strong curvature near a minimum indicates that small weight changes will significantly affect the loss, guiding the allocation of higher precision to sensitive layers.

A Bayesian perspective on mixed‑precision quantization has been explored by methods that infer per‑tensor bit widths from the uncertainty of weights in a variational posterior. Although this approach provides a principled probabilistic treatment, it does not enforce explicit control over the resulting bit widths, which can lead to configurations that are suboptimal for hardware implementation.

Mixed‑precision search has also been framed as a neural architecture search problem. In one formulation, each layer maintains separate weight copies for every candidate bit width, and a stochastic variant of DARTS is employed to learn the optimal bit‑width assignment jointly with the network parameters. This strategy integrates bit‑width selection into the architecture optimization loop.

Reinforcement‑learning based methods treat bit‑width assignment as a decision problem. An agent observes layer‑level characteristics and selects a bit width from a discrete action space; after a brief fine‑tuning phase, the validation accuracy serves as a reward. Some designs augment the reward with direct feedback from target hardware, enabling the agent to adapt to device‑specific constraints without relying on proxy metrics.

Independent works have shown that learning the quantization scale together with model parameters improves fixed‑bit‑width networks. By redefining the quantization operation to expose a learnable scale, these methods jointly optimize scale and weights. Extending RVQ to neural networks, weight compression methods store only the centroids of K‑means‑quantized vectors, achieving substantial model size reductions. Our contribution primarily advances the group‑fairness literature by defining unfairness as the optimal‑transport distance from a classifier’s score function to the set of all group‑fair score functions. Because the transport cost is evaluated on the original feature space, the same formulation also implicitly accounts for individual similarity, thereby offering a bridge between the two fairness paradigms and opening a pathway for future refinements that could further improve individual‑fairness guarantees.

Methods for mitigating unfairness are commonly grouped into preprocessing (altering the data), postprocessing (adjusting predictions), and in‑processing (modifying the learning algorithm). While preprocessing and postprocessing techniques treat fairness as an external correction, we embed fairness directly into the training objective. By introducing a differentiable optimal‑transport regularizer, OTF can be added to any standard loss function, allowing the model to learn fair representations end‑to‑end. This positions our work firmly within the in‑processing family, but distinguishes it from prior in‑processing approaches that rely on heuristic constraints or ad‑hoc penalty terms.

A line of in‑processing work projects an unfair model onto the feasible set defined by fairness constraints, typically measuring the projection distance with Kullback‑Leibler (KL) divergence. Although KL‑based projections are analytically convenient, they ignore the geometry of the feature space and therefore cannot exploit similarity information among individuals. Our method replaces the KL divergence with an optimal‑transport cost, which respects the underlying metric on the data and yields a principled notion of the minimal “work” required to achieve fairness. This geometric perspective is a core contribution of our approach.

Optimal‑transport has also been applied to fairness, most notably through barycenter constructions that move each demographic distribution toward a common reference. Barycenter‑based methods have been used for preprocessing, classification, and regression, but they impose strong restrictions: the fairness notion must be expressible as exact equality of group distributions, the cost must be a metric, and extending to continuous or multiple sensitive attributes is cumbersome. In contrast, OTF works with a broad class of linear fairness constraints, accommodates categorical and continuous protected variables simultaneously, and permits arbitrary, user‑defined cost functions. Moreover, we derive an entropically regularized formulation that is efficiently computable and fully differentiable, addressing the scalability limitations of earlier OT‑fairness techniques.

Building on this idea, we introduce a tractable, regularized OT projection that can be embedded as a training regularizer. This enables the optimizer to directly minimize the unfairness cost during learning, rather than merely evaluating it post‑hoc, and empirically yields a superior trade‑off between predictive accuracy and fairness across a range of conditional fairness criteria such as equalized odds.

[ANSWER]: Confidence estimation has attracted extensive attention because it enables reliable failure prediction and out‑of‑distribution detection in deployed systems. Early work on calibration focused on classification models, where techniques such as temperature scaling and Dirichlet‑based methods have become standard. In the context of neural machine translation, only a handful of studies have examined calibration. Prior analyses reported that NMT models appear well‑calibrated during training but become severely miscalibrated at inference time, especially for decisions such as predicting sentence termination. These works, however, stop at diagnosing the problem and do not provide a practical solution that can be integrated into modern Transformer‑based translators. In contrast, our approach introduces a learned confidence estimator that is trained jointly with the translation model, requires no additional supervision, and can be incorporated into any standard NMT architecture without degrading translation quality. By interpreting confidence as the number of “hints” the model requests, we obtain a direct, interpretable signal that is tightly coupled to the model’s own decision process.

Monte‑Carlo dropout and other Bayesian approximations have been proposed to capture predictive uncertainty in NMT. While effective at revealing model variance, these methods incur substantial computational overhead because they require multiple forward passes at test time and are sensitive to the choice of dropout rate. Our method sidesteps these limitations by learning a single‑shot confidence score from the decoder’s hidden states. This score can be computed with the same cost as a standard forward pass, making it suitable for large‑scale or latency‑sensitive translation services. Empirically, the confidence estimates produced by our model outperform dropout‑based uncertainty measures on both sentence‑level and word‑level quality estimation benchmarks.

Supervised quality estimation (QE) models aim to predict translation quality without references, but they typically rely on large amounts of manually annotated quality scores, which are expensive to collect and often unavailable for low‑resource language pairs. Consequently, supervised QE remains impractical for many real‑world deployments. Our work contributes an unsupervised alternative that leverages internal signals of the NMT system itself. By using the learned confidence estimator as an intrinsic quality proxy, we achieve higher correlation with human judgments than existing unsupervised QE metrics, while avoiding the need for any external annotations or repeated stochastic sampling.

Beyond providing a reliable confidence metric, we exploit the estimated confidence to guide instance‑specific label smoothing during training. Existing label‑smoothing techniques apply a uniform smoothing factor across all training examples, ignoring the varying difficulty of individual sentences. By scaling the smoothing mass according to the model’s confidence, our confidence‑based label smoothing adapts to the intrinsic uncertainty of each instance and consistently yields better translation performance than the standard uniform approach across multiple benchmark datasets (e.g., WMT14 En‑De, NIST Zh‑En, WMT16 Ro‑En, IWSLT14 De‑En). This demonstrates that our confidence estimator not only serves as a diagnostic tool but also enhances the core training objective of NMT systems.

With the rise of deep learning, neural approaches have become predominant and can be grouped into three families. Neural transition‑based parsers construct the graph incrementally by predicting a sequence of parsing actions. Sequence‑to‑graph parsers first encode the input sentence and then generate graph structures directly, often using graph‑generation modules. Sequence‑to‑sequence parsers linearize the AMR graph into a string and treat parsing as a standard text‑to‑text generation problem. More recently, pretrained language models such as BERT have been incorporated to provide richer sentence representations, and models have been further pretrained on related seq2seq tasks (e.g., machine translation, syntactic parsing) before fine‑tuning on AMR parsing. These works demonstrate that leveraging large‑scale textual pretraining improves parsing accuracy, but they focus on adapting models that were pretrained solely on textual data and typically require auxiliary tasks to inject structural knowledge.

Research on AMR‑to‑text generation also falls into two main categories. Graph‑to‑sequence models employ a dedicated graph encoder to ingest the AMR structure and a sequential decoder to produce fluent sentences. In contrast, sequence‑to‑sequence models first linearize the AMR graph and then apply either randomly initialized or pretrained seq2seq architectures. Recent efforts have explored integrating AMR information into pretrained transformers, for example by adding adapter modules to T5, thereby enhancing generation quality. However, these approaches generally do not involve pretraining on graph data themselves and are limited to generation, as they assume the full AMR graph is available at inference time.

In this work we introduce a graph‑self‑supervised pretraining paradigm that augments pretrained language models with structural awareness of AMR graphs. Two graph auto‑encoding strategies are proposed for graph‑to‑graph pretraining, and four auxiliary tasks are designed to jointly train on textual and graph inputs, enabling seamless combination of text‑to‑text and graph‑to‑graph objectives. A unified training framework bridges the gap between pretraining and downstream fine‑tuning for both AMR parsing (text‑to‑graph) and AMR‑to‑text generation (graph‑to‑text). Leveraging large‑scale silver AMR data further enhances the self‑supervised signals, and experiments show that this approach yields state‑of‑the‑art results on standard benchmarks, improves robustness to domain shift, and constitutes the first methodology to perform self‑supervised pretraining directly on semantic graphs.

This difficulty has motivated a line of work that seeks to learn the reward function from social input, either by allowing humans to provide reward signals directly or by inferring reward structure from human behavior.  Direct reward‑signal approaches face the challenge that people rarely produce the scalar reinforcement signals assumed by traditional algorithms, and they often rely on the simplifying assumption that the expert behaves optimally without considering the learning process of the agent.

A substantial body of research addresses reward inference from observed actions using inverse reinforcement learning (IRL).  Early IRL methods infer a reward function that rationalizes expert demonstrations, but they suffer from fundamental identifiability problems because many reward functions can explain the same behavior.  To mitigate this ambiguity, active query strategies have been proposed that let the learner pose questions to the human and incorporate the answers into the reward estimate.  An alternative line of work strengthens the underlying assumption by treating the human as an intentional teacher who deliberately selects demonstrations to facilitate learning.

Instructional language—utterances that prescribe specific actions or goals—has been explored as a means of communicating preferences to agents.  In reinforcement‑learning contexts, instructions have been used to shape policy learning, to guide exploration, and to serve as indirect evidence of latent reward preferences.  Several studies have extended IRL‑style inference to handle instruction inputs, demonstrating that agents can generalize from a limited set of command‑like utterances to broader task specifications.  Theoretical analyses of when and how instructions should be employed, relative to other forms of linguistic input, remain an active area of investigation.

Descriptive language, which conveys abstract information about the reward structure rather than concrete action directives, has attracted growing interest.  Researchers have investigated learning reward functions from existing textual corpora, from interactive free‑form dialogue, and from narrative descriptions that encode domain knowledge.  While such approaches can capture rich, context‑sensitive information, they introduce a grounding problem: mapping high‑level linguistic concepts onto the agent’s perception and action spaces.  Some work sidesteps this issue by assuming predefined groundings, thereby enabling a clearer analysis of the informational value of reward‑descriptive language.  Related studies have also examined descriptive statements about agent behavior, using them to shape task representations or to drive exploration, though these efforts typically focus on behavior‑centred rather than environment‑centred descriptions.

The assumption that training data are generated by a neutral demonstrator has been challenged by research on pedagogical teaching.  Within this line, the Rational Speech Act (RSA) framework formalizes communication as recursive Bayesian reasoning, drawing on Gricean principles of informativeness and relevance.  RSA‑based models have been applied to a variety of language tasks, including reference games, image captioning, and instruction following, showing that agents can exploit the intentionality of human teachers to improve inference.  Extending this perspective to reinforcement learning, several recent works propose pragmatic algorithms that treat observed data—whether demonstrations, reward signals, or language—as deliberately informative.  Inverse reward design (IRD) exemplifies this approach by interpreting supplied reward functions as clues about the true underlying preferences, thereby reducing alignment risk. [ANSWER]: Research on efficient computation of probabilistic queries has a long history in machine learning and artificial intelligence, originating with exact inference methods for multivariate graphical models. In this setting, queries are typically divided into two categories. Conditional probability queries ask for the probability of a subset of variables of interest given observed values for another subset, marginalizing over the remaining variables. Assignment queries seek the most likely assignment of values for a set of variables under the same conditioning; these are often referred to as most probable explanation (MPE) queries, or as maximum a posteriori (MAP) queries when the set of marginalized variables is empty.

When a model exhibits a sparse Markov dependence structure, a substantial body of work has developed inference algorithms that exploit this sparsity. Autoregressive neural sequence models, however, are inherently non‑Markovian: the real‑valued hidden state at each step depends on the entire history of the sequence, and each hidden state defines a branching tree of exponentially many future trajectories with state‑dependent probabilities. Consequently, the dynamic‑programming strategies that are effective for Markov‑structured models do not apply, and both conditional probability and assignment queries are known to be NP‑hard in the general case.

A considerable amount of research in natural‑language processing has addressed assignment‑type queries for neural sequence models, especially the MAP problem of generating high‑probability sequences conditioned on prior context or auxiliary information. Various heuristic decoding methods have been proposed and widely adopted, including beam search, best‑first search, sampling‑based approaches, and hybrid variants that combine elements of these strategies. While such decoding techniques can be employed to approximate conditional probabilities, they fundamentally produce lower bounds on the quantities of interest and therefore serve as biased estimators. This limitation has motivated investigations into alternative methods for more accurate probability estimation in the context of neural sequence models.

Early large‑scale collections such as ImageNet demonstrated that growing data volume can simultaneously introduce subtle correlations, for example background cues that leak object class information. In the context of visual question answering, several methods train an auxiliary classifier on the question modality and use its predictions to regularize the main model, either by masking softmax outputs, employing product‑of‑experts formulations, or jointly optimizing a full model together with a question‑only expert. These strategies share the reliance on a subset classifier to expose and attenuate the influence of biased cues. While effective at limiting shortcut learning, they differ from methods that evaluate bias by directly perturbing input modalities after training.

Feature‑importance and interpretability techniques provide complementary insights into model behavior at the level of individual inputs. The perceptual score also enables a fine‑grained bias analysis by decomposing the overall reliance into contributions from specific data subsets, such as question types. Early work such as [1]–[4] highlighted obfuscation transformations as a source of adversarial examples for downstream models, but did not address the problem of selecting an optimal subset of transformations to maximally deceive a target model. An earlier method [9] used a Metropolis‑Hastings algorithm to find optimal variable‑name replacements, representing a less efficient alternative to the first‑order techniques of [6]. Robust training strategies that aim to mitigate adversarial effects have been investigated as well. [10] introduced a defense that trains models to abstain when uncertain about potentially perturbed inputs; the method searches a small, greedily explored transformation space and is tailored to tasks that require only limited program context (e.g., variable‑type prediction), making extension to whole‑program tasks such as summarization non‑trivial.

Building on the local‑perturbation paradigm, [11] expanded the set of permissible transformations and adopted a standard min‑max formulation for adversarial training. [ANSWER]: Predicting sets with a simple multilayer perceptron (MLP) decoder has been widely adopted for tasks such as point‑cloud generation [1, 2], bounding‑box prediction [3, 4], and graph construction (sets of nodes and edges) [5, 6]. These approaches output an ordered list and treat it as if it were unordered, which gives rise to the responsibility problem. Some point‑cloud methods mitigate this issue by imposing domain‑specific assumptions, for example assuming independence of points within a set [7] or exploiting grid‑like structures [8]. To avoid the computational cost of graph‑matching losses, permutation‑invariant losses have been computed in latent space, for instance by comparing graphs adversarially [9].

Another line of work employs recurrent neural network (RNN) decoders to generate the list representation [10‑12]. When a canonical ordering can be derived from domain knowledge, the set prediction problem simplifies to a sequence problem [12]; an example is the generation of graph nodes ordered by a breadth‑first‑search traversal [13].

Iterative energy‑minimisation approaches have also been explored. Mordatch [14] introduced a method that iteratively minimises an energy function within each forward pass and differentiates through the iteration to learn network parameters. This technique has been demonstrated on small 2‑D element sets, showing the feasibility of differentiable optimisation loops for set‑structured outputs. Zhang et al. [15] constructed an auto‑encoder that pools a set into a feature vector and shares encoder information with a permutation‑equivariant decoder, thereby avoiding the responsibility problem; however, the requirement of an encoder at inference time restricts the approach to auto‑encoding rather than open‑set prediction. Greff et al. [16] proposed an auto‑encoder with a set‑structured latent space for images, enabling the discovery of latent object sets under task‑specific assumptions, which is of interest for representation learning.

The idea of using back‑propagation through an optimisation process as a decoder originates from introspective neural networks [17, 18], where the optimisation loops for prediction and weight learning are performed sequentially. Subsequent work on nested optimisation for structured outputs [19, 20] generalises this concept, allowing the outer optimisation to differentiate through the inner optimisation. Related studies also differentiate through optimisation procedures, as in [14] and [16], highlighting the broader applicability of such techniques to set‑valued outputs. In contrast, differentiating through a decoder to learn representations rather than predictions has been investigated in [21].

It is useful to distinguish vector‑to‑set settings from set‑to‑set mappings. Equivariant variants of Deep Sets [22] and self‑attention mechanisms [23] address set‑to‑set transformations, where the output ordering typically mirrors the input and the responsibility problem does not arise. Methods that predict permutation matrices for sets, effectively converting a set to a list, have been studied in [24, 25]. These approaches require an input set, whereas vector‑to‑set models are necessary for tasks such as object detection, where the input is a feature vector derived from an image encoder and must be transformed into an output set.

Knowledge‑graph reasoning extends this setting to multi‑hop scenarios in which many edges or nodes may be unobserved, and queries can involve paths, conjunctions, disjunctions, or arbitrary combinations of logical operators.  Formal definitions of reasoning over knowledge graphs have been provided in several surveys, which describe the problem as constructing new triples that are not present in the original graph while respecting the underlying relational structure.

A large body of work addresses multi‑hop query answering through embedding‑based methods.  Early approaches such as Graph Query Embeddings (GQE) projected queries and entities into a shared vector space using simple linear operators, enabling efficient nearest‑neighbor retrieval for path and conjunctive queries.  Query2Box introduced a box‑shaped representation that captures set‑like semantics and supports conjunctions and existential quantification, while BetaE extended this idea with probabilistic embeddings to model both conjunctive and disjunctive queries.  Subsequent extensions incorporated additional logical operators, but most of these models were limited to existential‑positive first‑order logic and could not represent negation.  The primary distinction among these methods lies in how they encode query structures, the geometric objects used for set representation, and the range of logical operators they support.

Beyond embedding techniques, a variety of alternative paradigms have been explored for knowledge‑graph reasoning. [ANSWER]: Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) builds on the success of macro‑operators and abstraction in classical planning, inspiring a substantial body of work that decomposes control across multiple levels of abstraction.  Early approaches emphasized the intuitive benefits of such decompositions—simpler sub‑problems and the ability to make long‑term decisions—but more recent analyses have highlighted that, for modern neural‑network‑based agents, the principal advantage of HRL often lies in its enhanced exploration capabilities.  By separating the acquisition of low‑level policies (options or skills) from high‑level decision making, HRL can dramatically accelerate learning on downstream tasks.

A diverse set of methods has been proposed for discovering low‑level primitives.  Some techniques rely on random walk data to identify useful behaviours, while others formulate mutual‑information objectives that encourage diversity among options.  Additional strands of research exploit datasets of agent or expert trajectories, motion‑capture recordings, or dedicated pre‑training tasks to shape the skill space.  These approaches differ in the source of supervision and the assumptions they make about the environment, yet they share the goal of producing reusable behaviours that can be composed by higher‑level policies.

The usefulness of learned skills across many downstream tasks is constrained by a trade‑off between generality and specificity.  Many prior works resolve this trade‑off in favour of specificity, often by selecting benchmark domains that align closely with the induced prior.  Classic navigation problems in grid‑world mazes and simulated robotic locomotion tasks dominate the evaluation landscape, where translating the robot’s centre of mass is the primary required skill.  In such settings, skills are frequently defined by partitioning the state space according to the agent’s position or by leveraging position‑heavy reward signals, thereby embedding an explicit locomotion prior.  Other studies that address non‑navigation environments introduce tailored pre‑training objectives or rely on in‑domain motion‑capture data to bias skill acquisition toward particular behaviours.

In contrast, recent efforts have begun to explore skill discovery without external supervision or task‑specific pre‑training designs, aiming to learn low‑level behaviours that do not encode a fixed bias toward any single type of motion.  These works seek to retain flexibility in the skill set, allowing downstream tasks to select the most appropriate behaviours dynamically rather than being constrained by a predetermined prior.  

Building on these lines of research, the present work proposes an unsupervised pre‑training framework that generates a hierarchy of skills with increasing complexity, each controlling a variable subset of the robot’s configuration.  A three‑level hierarchical policy is introduced to automatically select among these skills, determine target configurations, and execute the corresponding low‑level actions, thereby enabling dynamic trade‑offs between generality and specificity during downstream learning.  To evaluate the approach, a benchmark suite of sparse‑reward tasks for bipedal robots is released, extending assessment beyond traditional navigation problems and facilitating systematic comparison of motor‑skill and HRL methods.  Extensive experiments demonstrate how prior knowledge embedded in skills affects exploration efficiency, and show that the proposed hierarchical skill framework achieves superior performance relative to existing unsupervised skill discovery and hierarchical RL baselines.

The first strand focuses on worst‑case (or best‑case) scenarios, studying the expressive power of a given architecture. These works highlight the theoretical capacity of deep models to represent highly intricate functions that shallow counterparts cannot express.  

A second strand points out that a substantial gap may exist between the functions that are expressible by an architecture and those that are learnable in practice.  Average‑case analyses have demonstrated that certain functions, despite being representable, are provably hard to learn [9] or are vanishingly unlikely to be realised by random initialisations [10], [11], [12].  Conversely, some functions that are easily learned by deep networks can already be represented by shallow ones [13].  For arithmetic circuits, worst‑case and average‑case behaviours are more aligned, yet a pronounced gap remains between the matricisation rank of functions computed by deep versus shallow architectures [14].  

Within the context of ReLU networks, several average‑case studies have examined geometric distortion measures.  Works such as [15] and [16] argued that the expected length distortion of a curve under a random ReLU network grows exponentially with depth, while [17] provided a similar analysis for curvature of output trajectories.  These conclusions rely on weight initialisations that also induce exponentially large activations and exploding gradients [18], [19], conditions that are avoided by the commonly used He‑normal initialisation [20].  

A further line of research seeks complexity measures that correlate with generalisation performance.  Proposals based on classification margins [22], network compressibility [23] and PAC‑Bayes bounds [24] have been explored, aiming to connect structural or information‑theoretic properties of trained models with their ability to generalise.

Empirical experiments confirm that these theoretical predictions persist after training, demonstrating that length and volume distortion remain controlled in practical settings. To mitigate these issues, DAgger [2] introduced a no‑regret online imitation approach that requires access to corrective oracle actions. More recent LfD methods favor inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) [3], which infers a reward function that renders expert behavior optimal, allowing standard reinforcement learning algorithms to be applied [4, 5]. A prominent IRL instance is Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL) [6], which casts imitation as distribution matching and employs a GAN‑style discriminator to minimize the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the state‑action distributions of the expert and the learner [7]. Subsequent work extended GAIL by adopting alternative RL frameworks [8] or employing different divergence measures [9‑11]; most of these approaches rely on on‑policy learning, which can be sample‑inefficient.

Off‑policy extensions aim to improve sample efficiency. DAC [8] reuses past transitions stored in a replay buffer rather than generating on‑policy data, while similar ideas appear in [12]. These methods, however, often overlook the discrepancy introduced when substituting the on‑policy distribution with off‑policy approximations, leading to deviations from the intended objective. ValueDICE [13] adapts the DICE formulation [14] to obtain an off‑policy LfD objective, but it requires access to expert actions, limiting its applicability in model‑free settings where actions are unavailable.

Learning from Observations (LfO) addresses the more challenging setting where only expert states are provided. Forward‑model methods learn a dynamics model to predict next states, enabling policy learning for finite‑horizon tasks [18, 19]; however, they may not scale to long or infinite horizons. Inverse‑model approaches learn a mapping from state transitions to actions, exemplified by Behavior Cloning from Observations (BCO) [20], which first infers missing actions and then applies behavior cloning. This strategy inherits the challenges of BC and does not guarantee accurate action recovery unless the underlying MDP is deterministic and injective. Additional lines of work consider mismatched transition dynamics [22] or differing observation viewpoints [21, 23, 24]. Comprehensive surveys of LfO methods are provided in [25].

Lyapunov drift has been used as a fundamental design and analysis tool in many problems, including the wireless scheduling problem [10], [11], fair resource allocation among competing users [7], [8], and stochastic game theory [12]. Based on Lyapunov‑drift methods, stochastic dynamic optimization algorithms using the drift‑plus‑penalty technique have been widely applied in queueing and networking problems (see [13] and references therein). Existing Lyapunov optimization methods are predominantly opportunistic, assuming that random quantities (such as completion time, reward, system state) are observed before decision‑making at each stage, or that the first‑ and second‑order statistics of these quantities are known. In many applications these assumptions are violated, motivating approaches that learn the underlying statistics while optimizing objectives such as total utility. [ANSWER]: Most continual learning approaches are formulated for the class‑incremental setting, where a model is trained on disjoint sets of classes that arrive in successive increments and is evaluated on all classes learned so far. Early methods mitigate catastrophic forgetting by storing a subset of exemplars from previously seen classes and replaying them together with new data (e.g., iCaRL, GEM). Although effective, exemplar storage scales poorly because memory capacity becomes a bottleneck as the number of classes grows. To avoid explicit replay, regularization‑based techniques such as Elastic Weight Consolidation and Synaptic Intelligence constrain updates to important parameters, thereby reducing forgetting without additional storage. These methods, however, typically lag behind replay‑based approaches in accuracy. More recent work on few‑shot class‑incremental learning (FSCIL) tackles the additional challenge of learning new categories from only a few labeled examples while maintaining a limited memory budget. Despite these advances, the majority of CL methods assume that the full training set for each increment is available and fully labeled, an assumption that conflicts with the streaming, often unlabeled data encountered in real‑world robotic deployments where online learning is required.

Active learning research has focused on reducing labeling effort by allowing models to query the most informative unlabeled instances. A common strategy is uncertainty sampling, where predictive entropy, margin, or variance is used to select samples for annotation. Recent deep‑learning‑based active learning methods augment the training objective with auxiliary loss terms that encourage well‑calibrated uncertainty estimates. Nonetheless, these approaches are designed for batch learning: the model is trained on a static labeled set before querying, and the learned classifier is not updated continually. When applied in a continual setting, such methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting because they lack mechanisms to preserve knowledge of earlier tasks. Moreover, traditional active learning pipelines assume a closed‑world scenario; they can detect unknown classes only in the initial batch, after which newly encountered unknowns are forced into previously learned categories, eroding the ability to recognize novel objects in later increments.
