Early approaches relied on training each candidate from scratch, incurring prohibitive computational costs. To alleviate this, weight‑sharing schemes were introduced, whereby subnetworks sampled from a supernet inherit shared parameters. Although this dramatically reduces training time, subsequent analyses revealed a weak correlation between the shared‑weight performance and the true ranking of architectures, causing instability even in modest search spaces. Further investigations highlighted that inaccurate evaluation can render NAS essentially random. More recent zero‑cost methods attempt to score architectures using only the initial random weights and a single forward–backward pass, offering substantial speedups. However, their predictive power deteriorates in larger benchmarks such as NASBench‑101, where they struggle to distinguish high‑performing models. Complementary to algorithmic advances, curated benchmarks containing fully trained networks for all architectures in a given search space have been released, enabling the community to isolate and compare search strategies under controlled evaluation conditions.

The expense of evaluating architectures on target tasks has motivated the use of proxy tasks and datasets. A common practice is to search on a small, well‑studied dataset (e.g., CIFAR‑10) and then transfer the discovered architecture to a larger, more demanding benchmark (e.g., ImageNet). Empirical studies have examined how well performance on one classification dataset predicts performance on others, reporting varying degrees of transferability across both supervised and unsupervised settings. Analyses on NASBench‑201 quantified ranking correlations across multiple datasets, while other work explored transfer across task modalities. Despite these efforts, even training on a reduced proxy dataset typically requires several epochs of full training, limiting the overall efficiency gains that proxy‑based NAS can achieve.

Self‑supervised learning has emerged as an alternative avenue for architecture evaluation without reliance on labeled data. By constructing surrogate objectives from automatically generated pseudo‑labels, researchers have leveraged tasks such as rotation prediction, colorization, and solving jigsaw puzzles to assess network quality. These proxy tasks have been employed to rank architectures and guide search, demonstrating that unsupervised signals can capture useful representational capacities. Nevertheless, most existing self‑supervised evaluations still adopt classification‑oriented objectives and require processing the entire dataset, leaving open questions about the optimality of the chosen tasks and the potential benefits of alternative supervision signals.

In this work we introduce a generic NAS framework that departs from classification‑based evaluation and instead employs a regression‑driven proxy task built on manually designed synthetic signal bases. By training architectures to regress onto these task‑agnostic signals, the method directly measures intrinsic representation power, fully exploits every training sample, and eliminates the need for task‑specific labels. A lightweight automated search identifies the most suitable combination of synthetic bases for a given search space, further enhancing correlation with downstream performance. Extensive experiments across thirteen convolutional and one language modeling search space demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves substantially higher ranking correlations (Spearman’s ρ) with the true downstream accuracies while requiring only a single batch of unlabeled data and a few seconds of training. Compared with weight‑sharing, zero‑cost, and self‑supervised classification proxies, the regression‑based strategy delivers orders‑of‑magnitude speedups and consistently discovers top‑performing architectures, establishing a new baseline for efficient, task‑agnostic neural architecture search.

These environments feature a clear demonstration/execution split, but they are limited to simplistic, discrete dynamics and a small set of task concepts. MAGICAL extends this line of work to continuous control and richer visual observations while preserving the demonstration/test split, thereby offering a more challenging and realistic testbed for algorithms that must extrapolate demonstrator intent across combinatorial changes in the world. Dedicated imitation‑learning benchmarks such as [7, 8] focus on achieving high success rates on complex robotic tasks, yet they evaluate algorithms exclusively in the environment used for data collection. Consequently, they cannot reveal overfitting to context‑specific cues nor assess the ability to transfer intent to novel settings. [ANSWER]: Early ensemble‑distillation methods focused on reproducing only the average output of a teacher ensemble.  These works showed that a single neural network can be trained to mimic the mean predictions of a large collection of models, typically by minimizing a cross‑entropy loss against the ensemble’s soft targets or by using a convex combination of the teachers’ outputs.  While effective for improving speed at test time, such approaches do not preserve the variability among ensemble members, which limits their usefulness for uncertainty quantification.  Representative examples include the original demonstrations that a student network can learn the knowledge of a big ensemble, methods that augment the standard loss with a convex combination of teacher predictions, and online student‑teacher schemes where the teacher is obtained via Markov‑chain Monte‑Carlo training.  

Subsequent research introduced techniques aimed at capturing the diversity of the teacher ensemble.  Ensemble Distribution Distillation (EnDD) was among the first to model the full predictive distribution by fitting a Dirichlet‑parameterized network to the ensemble outputs.  Building on this idea, later works also assumed a Dirichlet form for the predictive distribution, learning separate networks for the Dirichlet mean (class probabilities) and concentration (confidence).  To mitigate over‑confidence and low diversity on the training set, these methods employed unsupervised auxiliary data and temperature‑annealing schedules.  Although these approaches improve uncertainty estimates, they remain restricted to classification tasks and rely on the Dirichlet assumption, which can be overly limiting for more general predictive scenarios.  

Another line of work extended the basic distillation framework by assigning each teacher member a dedicated task head while sharing a common backbone.  In this setting the backbone learns a shared representation, and each head is trained to reproduce the predictions of a specific ensemble member using standard cross‑entropy loss.  Weight‑sharing strategies such as BatchEnsemble have also been incorporated, together with data‑perturbation schemes—including Gaussian noise, Output‑Diversified Sampling (ODS), and confidence‑aware ODS—to increase diversity among the heads on the training data.  These perturbation‑based methods, however, introduce additional computational overhead because they require per‑iteration generation of adversarial‑like perturbations, making training slower and less scalable to large ensembles.  

In contrast, the proposed approach introduces a flexible functional ensemble distillation framework that captures both the predictive mean and the full covariance structure of the teacher ensemble without restricting the predictive distribution to a Dirichlet form.  By transferring stochasticity to a latent noise variable, the distilled model can generate diverse function samples and compute inter‑prediction covariances, which are valuable for downstream tasks such as correlated object‑detection decisions.  To address the common over‑fitting regime where ensemble members achieve near‑zero training loss yet exhibit divergent test‑time behavior, the method leverages mixup augmentation to create an auxiliary dataset that is both sufficiently different from the original training set to elicit diverse teacher predictions and sufficiently close to preserve performance on the target domain.  This auxiliary data is generated without requiring any external unlabeled samples, keeping the pipeline simple and scalable.  Extensive experiments on several image‑classification benchmarks demonstrate that the resulting distilled model attains superior accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty estimation compared with prior ensemble‑distillation techniques, while remaining computationally efficient at inference time.

Clause‑based approaches [5] navigate dependency trees to split sentences into simpler, independent segments.  

Several prior works have addressed the clustering of noun phrases (NPs) and relation phrases (RPs) into coherent groups. A traditional method for NP canonicalization maps mentions to an existing knowledge base (e.g., Wikidata), a task commonly referred to as entity linking [6]. This approach faces difficulties when many NPs refer to entities absent from the target knowledge base, leaving them uncategorized.  

The RESOLVER system [7] clusters phrases using string‑similarity features. Subsequent work [8] employs manually defined features for NP canonicalization and then clusters relation phrases. Concept Resolver [9] adopts a “one sense per category’’ assumption to cluster NP mentions in NELL, requiring an additional schema of relation types. KB‑Unify [10] tackles the unification of multiple canonical and open knowledge graphs into a single graph, but depends on an external sense inventory that may not be available.  

The CESI architecture [11] treats canonicalization as a two‑step pipeline: first, it learns embeddings for NPs and RPs with the HolE algorithm [12]; second, it applies hierarchical agglomerative clustering to the learned embeddings to produce clusters.

[ANSWER]: The literature on learning with graph‑structured data can be divided into semi‑supervised methods that exploit node features and labels, and unsupervised embedding techniques that rely solely on the graph topology. Semi‑supervised approaches such as graph convolutional networks, spectral variants, and diffusion‑based models learn to propagate label information across edges (e.g., [3]–[9], [10]–[16]). Our method belongs to a different branch: it does not require any external supervision, and it learns representations by directly modelling the relationship between every pair of nodes through a trainable attention‑guided random walk. By eliminating the need for label information, we address scenarios where annotations are scarce or unavailable, positioning our work as a complementary alternative to the feature‑centric semi‑supervised family.

Unsupervised graph embedding methods aim to produce task‑agnostic node vectors that preserve structural proximity. Early techniques operate on the adjacency matrix ([18], [19]), while more recent models incorporate higher‑order connectivity via simulated walks or matrix factorisations ([20]–[22]). These approaches typically fix a context distribution—often defined by hand‑tuned hyper‑parameters such as walk length or window size—and then optimise an embedding objective. In contrast, our contribution is to replace these static hyper‑parameters with differentiable attention parameters that are learned end‑to‑end. By back‑propagating through the expected random‑walk distribution, we automatically discover the optimal context for each graph, which empirically matches or surpasses manually tuned baselines across diverse networks.

Attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of many deep learning domains, guiding models toward the most informative parts of the input in language, vision, and video analysis (e.g., [23]–[26]). Prior graph‑related work has employed attention to weight neighbour contributions during message passing, but the attention weights are used only at inference time. Our approach diverges fundamentally: the attention parameters are attached to the data‑generation process itself, shaping the random‑walk sampling that underlies the embedding learning. This novel use of attention to steer the training distribution—not the predictor—makes our method the first to integrate attention directly into the stochastic process that defines graph context, thereby offering a new paradigm for unsupervised graph representation learning.

The approach can be attached to existing keypoint detectors with minimal architectural changes and computational overhead. [ANSWER]: The design of sample‑efficient sequential decision‑making agents has long been grounded in principled approaches to information acquisition and information representation. Early work demonstrated how information‑theoretic tools, particularly rate‑distortion theory, can formalize the trade‑off between the amount of information an agent must gather and the performance loss incurred by adopting a simplified learning target. By interpreting the complexity of a learning problem as the number of bits required to identify a target, these studies provided a theoretical foundation for constructing satisficing objectives that balance efficiency and near‑optimality.

A central difficulty in achieving sample efficiency is the exploration–exploitation dilemma that arises in multi‑armed bandit settings. The information‑directed sampling (IDS) principle was introduced as a systematic way to navigate this dilemma. IDS defines an information ratio as the squared expected regret divided by the expected information gain, and prescribes selecting the policy that minimizes this ratio at each timestep. This framework yields elegant theoretical guarantees and has been extended in numerous directions, including refined analyses of the information ratio, adaptations to contextual and combinatorial bandits, and connections to posterior sampling methods. However, the majority of IDS‑based research measures information gain exclusively with respect to the optimal action, thereby limiting its applicability when the learning objective extends beyond a single optimal policy.

Rate‑distortion concepts have been operationalized in sequential decision‑making through the Blahut‑Arimoto algorithm, which provides an alternating‑optimization procedure for computing optimal trade‑offs between information cost and distortion. The algorithm has been widely studied in the information‑theory literature for its convergence properties, computational efficiency, and extensions to various channel models. In the bandit context, the Blahut‑Arimoto approach has enabled agents to compute satisficing targets that adapt as more data are collected, but prior implementations have primarily combined these targets with probability‑matching action selection such as Thompson sampling, leaving the integration with more sophisticated information‑acquisition strategies unexplored.

Leveraging the Blahut‑Arimoto algorithm to obtain dynamic learning targets, we redefine the information ratio to capture expected regret and information gain about these targets, thereby extending IDS beyond the optimal‑action focus. The resulting algorithm, which we term Blahut‑Arimoto Information‑Directed Sampling (BLAIDS), retains a single real‑valued hyperparameter that governs the designer’s preference for target fidelity versus learning speed. We provide a computationally tractable instantiation of BLAIDS that mirrors the efficiency gains observed in prior Blahut‑Arimoto‑based methods while inheriting the stronger exploration guarantees of IDS. Theoretical analysis establishes regret bounds that reflect the combined effect of target compression and directed information acquisition, and extensive experiments on multi‑armed bandit benchmarks demonstrate that BLAIDS outperforms both standard IDS and Blahut‑Arimoto‑guided Thompson sampling across a range of distortion levels. This work therefore bridges the gap between rate‑distortion‑based target design and optimal information‑directed exploration, offering a flexible and principled tool for constructing sample‑efficient agents in complex environments.

ANSWER: Previous studies on TDMR (Task-Dataset-Metric-Result) extraction primarily rely on data sources such as NLP-progress or PapersWithCode. While these sources are popular, they lack rigorous quality control, including standardized TDM entity representation and complete publication coverage. Some efforts, such as [1] and [2], go further by extracting TDM triples and result values, and normalizing them for leaderboard construction. However, these approaches are constrained by their reliance on a closed domain, requiring extracted triples to match a pre-defined TDM taxonomy. Other studies, such as [3] and [4], only extract TDM triples without result values, thereby forgoing leaderboard construction. Meanwhile, [6] focuses on extracting result values, but only in the context of pre-defined TDM triples, making it similar in limitation to [1]. Consequently, these methods are not adaptable to the dynamic nature of emerging benchmarks, where new tasks, datasets, and metrics are frequently introduced.
In a parallel research thread, scientific leaderboards have been treated as a form of scientific knowledge graphs composed of Task, Dataset, and Metric entities. Information extraction in this context has been widely studied, as seen in works such as [5, 7, 8, 9, 10]. These studies typically focus on linking scientific content to structured entities but often assume that the schema or triples are known in advance.
In contrast to prior work, our approach addresses several critical limitations. We construct our dataset manually from publications to ensure comprehensive TDMR annotations, rather than relying on incomplete or unstandardized third-party sources. We normalize TDMR tuples for accurate leaderboard construction and propose novel experimental settings that reflect realistic, dynamic scenarios, including cold-start conditions without any pre-defined TDM taxonomy. By simultaneously constructing a scientific knowledge graph and linking publications to it in an open-domain setting, our method is inherently adaptable to the evolving research landscape.

[ANSWER]: Memory‑based approaches address catastrophic forgetting by re‑introducing information from earlier tasks during the training of new ones.  Some methods store raw exemplars from previous datasets and interleave them with data from the current task, thereby preserving performance on earlier categories.  Other techniques retain only a subset of past examples or compress them into a small buffer and use gradient‑based criteria to reduce interference between the old and new objectives.  A related line of work trains generative models—such as GANs or autoencoders—to synthesize samples that approximate past data distributions, offering a memory‑efficient alternative to explicit storage.  Still‑another family saves feature representations of prior instances and learns transformations that map these stored features into the space of the current task, again limiting the amount of retained raw data.

Regularization‑ and architecture‑based strategies aim to limit how much a new task can modify the parameters that are important for previously learned problems.  Weight‑regularization methods add explicit penalties that keep critical weights close to their earlier values, while mask‑based techniques freeze selected subsets of the network during the learning of subsequent tasks.  Some works increase the model’s capacity by allocating additional parameters for each incoming task, often coupled with mechanisms that decide how to partition the expanded network.  Variants of this paradigm search for task‑specific pathways through a shared backbone, freezing the identified routes and restricting further adaptation, or employ specialized components such as hypernetworks, deep artificial neurons, or compositional structures to provide flexible, reusable modules across tasks.

Meta‑learning, the paradigm of “learning to learn,” has been incorporated into sequential and continual learning settings to improve adaptation to new tasks while mitigating forgetting.  Approaches have leveraged meta‑optimization to shape initializations that are amenable to rapid fine‑tuning on successive problems, or to construct instance‑level prototypes that guide weight updates in a way that preserves prior knowledge.  Several recent studies combine meta‑learning objectives with continual‑learning constraints, demonstrating that meta‑trained learners can exhibit reduced interference when presented with a stream of tasks.  However, most of these works focus on shaping the learning dynamics rather than maintaining an explicit, incrementally updated knowledge repository.

Weight‑conditioning mechanisms modify network parameters in a data‑dependent manner, often by using auxiliary signals to adapt layer outputs.  Techniques such as feature‑wise linear modulation normalize convolutional activations through learned scaling and shifting functions, while other methods condition convolutional responses on external inputs like questions in visual‑question‑answering systems.  These conditioning schemes provide a way to steer the network’s computation without permanently altering the underlying weights, yet they have typically been applied as isolated modules rather than as part of a larger framework for continual knowledge accumulation.

In this work we introduce a continual‑learning method that unifies the advantages of the aforementioned streams.  By employing a meta‑learning procedure we construct a shared knowledge base whose parameters are incrementally enriched as new tasks arrive, while a set of trainable masks implements a selective addressing mechanism that queries the most relevant subset of the base for each task.  This design simultaneously mitigates catastrophic forgetting through weight reusability, avoids the need for extensive replay buffers or generative replay, and circumvents the parameter explosion associated with naïve capacity expansion.  Empirical evaluation on standard benchmarks demonstrates state‑of‑the‑art accuracy improvements of more than ten percent on large‑scale splits, with near‑zero forgetting and using roughly half the parameters of competing methods.  An ablation study confirms that the learned masks effectively isolate task‑specific knowledge within the shared repository, validating the proposed synergy between meta‑learning‑driven knowledge accumulation and conditional weight selection.

[ANSWER]: Recent self‑supervised learning (SSL) research has been dominated by contrastive approaches, which achieve strong performance on downstream tasks by learning representations that distinguish positive pairs from a set of negatives. Many of these methods are rooted in noise‑contrastive estimation, where the latent data distribution is inferred by contrasting true samples with randomly or synthetically generated noise. A seminal contribution introduced the Info‑NCE objective for learning image representations through an auto‑regressive model that predicts future frames, inspiring subsequent work that improves computational efficiency and leverages multi‑view augmentations as additional positive examples. Because early contrastive methods relied on a limited number of negative instances, a memory‑bank mechanism was proposed to store previously seen representations and treat each entry as an independent class for instance discrimination. However, the static nature of the stored vectors can lead to inconsistency with the evolving encoder during training. This issue was addressed by sampling negatives from large batches, and further mitigated by using a momentum‑updated encoder to refresh the memory bank, thereby reducing representation drift. Other refinements combine pretext‑invariant objectives with contrastive learning or decompose the contrastive loss into explicit alignment and uniformity terms, offering complementary perspectives on how to shape the embedding space.

Parallel to contrastive SSL, knowledge distillation has been extensively studied as a means to transfer the capabilities of a large teacher model to a more compact student without sacrificing generalization. Early distillation methods focused on matching the teacher’s output logits, while later approaches explored richer forms of supervision, such as transferring attention maps, aligning feature‑map statistics, preserving probability distributions, or maximizing mutual information between teacher and student representations. Extensions of these ideas include contrastive relational distillation, which builds on contrastive frameworks to derive a lower bound on mutual information for the student. While much of the distillation literature targets task‑specific fine‑tuning—particularly for image classification—some works have investigated task‑agnostic distillation during the pre‑training stage for language models. Notable examples include DistilBERT, TinyBERT, and MobileBERT, which compress transformer‑based language encoders via distillation and demonstrate strong performance across diverse downstream tasks. Additional studies emphasize the benefits of smaller, faster models for natural language representation learning by applying various distillation strategies. Although these techniques have proven effective for compressing language models, comparable efforts for visual representation learning in the pre‑training phase remain limited, highlighting an emerging research direction in the intersection of SSL and model compression.
